Machine Learning 1.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) for text-to-SQL agents pays a query when its result matches the reference on one database. However, a wrong query can match by luck when the data lack the rows that expose its bug. We study a counterfactual-database (CF) reward that also runs the final query on a few hidden, code-generated copies of the database and pays only if all results match (strict form) or by the share matched (mean form). On 1,302 synthetic audit questions, the strict form lowers the share of buggy queries paid in full from 29.5% to 16.8% and of reward hacks from 54.1% to 1.9%, rejecting 0 of 2,847 correct queries; copies from a family-blind generator do about as well. In a controlled GRPO comparison on a 3.35B model with three seeds per arm, training on the mean form did not improve in-domain accuracy (8.4% vs 11.7%), because the two rewards disagreed on only 5-7% of rollouts; on Spider it gained 1.6 points. One seed reverses both signs, so single-seed reward comparisons mislead. Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards ; data, models, demo: https://huggingface.co/counterfactual-sql
Machine Learning 1.comment: 4 pages + references and appendix (12 pages total). Code: https://github.com/RishiiGamer2201/counterfactual-sql-rewards

Machine Learning 1.title: RAWPrism: A Three-Task Dataset and a Unified Model for RAW-Domain Image Fusion
Machine Learning 1.summary: Research on multi-exposure fusion (MEF), multi-focus fusion (MFF), and infrared-visible image fusion (IVIF) has largely focused on rendered RGB images, while unified fusion across these tasks in the RAW domain before image signal processing (ISP) remains relatively underexplored. To support research in this setting, we introduce the RAWPrism dataset, covering all three tasks, and the RAWPrism model, a lightweight unified multi-task fusion network. The RAWPrism dataset comprises 422 usable MEF scenes and 150 registered MFF pairs from our RAW captures, together with 1,500 FMB-derived IVIF samples, in which the visible RAW inputs are reconstructed by ReRAW and their RGB counterparts rendered by CycleISP. Scene-level partitions and task-specific rendering and scoring protocols connect these resources to method development and evaluation. To our knowledge, the RAWPrism model is the first to unify MEF, MFF, and IVIF directly in the RAW domain. It combines a CFA-aware representation, task-conditioned source gating, and a shared backbone to support all three tasks with one 3.58M-parameter checkpoint. Together, the dataset and model support the study of shared fusion mechanisms across exposure, focus, and spectral complementarity.

Machine Learning 1.title: Inverse Reinforcement Learning with State-Dependent Foresight for Human Decision-Making
Machine Learning 1.summary: Computational modeling of behavior represents individuals with a model fitted to their observed behavior and characterizes them through its parameters. Naturalistic tasks incorporate the complexity of real environments and yield high-dimensional behavioral trajectories. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) infers the latent reward function underlying these trajectories. Standard IRL, however, assumes effectively infinite-horizon planning, whereas human foresight is both bounded and state-dependent. Here we introduce SC-AIRL (State-Conditional Adversarial IRL), which builds these two cognitive properties into the planner. Per-depth policies share one reward but differ in how far ahead they sum it explicitly. A state-conditional router mixes them according to the current state. Across held-out episodes in pedestrian crossing and highway overtaking tasks, SC-AIRL improves imitation over Standard AIRL, raising top-1 accuracy from 0.549 to 0.647 and from 0.629 to 0.718, respectively, while more closely reproducing participant behavior in rollouts. Inferred planning depth correlates with self-reported anxiety and motor impulsivity. SC-AIRL thus reproduces human behavior more closely than Standard AIRL while providing an interpretable, model-derived measure of state-dependent foresight.

Machine Learning 1.title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
Machine Learning 1.summary: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.
Machine Learning 1.comment: Accepted at the 23rd Sound and Music Computing Conference (SMC), 2026

Machine Learning 1.title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Memory-Efficient Latent Chain-of-Thought with Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
Machine Learning 1.summary: Standard Transformers have a fixed computational depth, limiting their ability to generalize to tasks that require variable-depth reasoning. The usual remedy, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), spends tokens to reason, inflating the key--value cache, so memory becomes the limiting cost when reasoning is served over large query batches. We study a depth-recurrent Transformer that decouples computational depth from parameter count by iterating a shared-weight block, so that adding reasoning steps leaves peak inference memory unchanged and grows latency only linearly, with no token generation. Three ingredients support the recurrence over 20+ thinking steps: a silent thinking objective that supervises only the final output, LayerScale initialization, and an identity-biased gate that opens a gradient highway across steps. We characterize it on three compositional domains with decreasing structural bias: graph reachability (adjacency masking), nested boolean logic (relative positioning), and unstructured relational text (no structural positional cue). We find a \emph{computational frontier}: accuracy climbs once the thinking-step count meets the task's complexity, reaching near-perfect performance on the two structured tasks and a lower plateau on unstructured text. How it climbs depends on the structural bias---abruptly from chance on the graph task, gradually on the other two. Depth recurrence extrapolates beyond the training range: it succeeds on the graph task where fixed-depth models barely extrapolate, and on the two sequence tasks comes within two points of fixed-depth Transformers that use $4$--$6.4\times$ more parameters. On the graph task, whose adjacency mask makes propagation depth verifiable, intermediate per-step supervision---a standard recipe for deep iterative models---consistently \emph{harms} this extrapolation at widths $d \geq 256$. We release the code for reproducibility.

Machine Learning 1.title: Scaling and Cross-Simulation Generalization of Graph Neural Networks for Cosmic-Web Classification in CAMELS
Machine Learning 1.summary: Graph-based methods can classify galaxies by their dark-matter cosmic-web environments, but reliability beyond development simulations remains uncertain. Galaxy-formation models alter tracer populations and spatial distributions, potentially shifting graph features. We test how graph neural networks scale with independent training realizations and transfer across hydrodynamical simulations. Using the $z=0$ CAMELS IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites, we label galaxies with $M_\star>10^9\,M_\odot$ as void, sheet, filament or knot from the smoothed cold-dark-matter density field. We represent their spatial distributions as periodic Delaunay graphs with ten geometric descriptors. We compare a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and five graph neural networks (GNNs), including a local graph Transformer, under realization-grouped evaluation. Learning curves increase training data from 10 to 100 realizations, with validation and test boxes fixed. We test every source-to-target suite pairing on 100 unseen realizations per target suite. On this external holdout, the Transformer, GAT+ and EdgeConv reach mean per-realization macro-averaged F1 scores of $0.652$, $0.651$ and $0.642$, against $0.481$ for the MLP. The Transformer outperforms the MLP by 0.171, while the difference between the Transformer and GAT+ is not statistically significant. Voids remain the hardest class. Performance is higher in boxes with more selected galaxies and shorter Delaunay edges. Associations with cosmological and feedback parameters weaken after accounting for galaxy richness and void fraction. Our results benchmark the scaling and cross-simulation transfer of galaxy-graph classifiers, demonstrating the value of neighbourhood information and identifying tracer sampling as an important limitation for dark-matter web inference.

Machine Learning 1.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers
Machine Learning 1.summary: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.
Machine Learning 1.comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Code at https://github.com/a1bhinav/puzzling-bench and data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/puzzling-bench/puzzling-bench

Machine Learning 1.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
Machine Learning 1.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.
Machine Learning 1.comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 19 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://github.com/PriorLabs/matsci-bo-bench

Machine Learning 1.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
Machine Learning 1.summary: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

Machine Learning 1.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
Machine Learning 1.summary: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

Machine Learning 1.title: Interpretable identification of constitutive parameter field for three-dimensional heterogeneous and graded hyperelastic materials from full-field displacements
Machine Learning 1.summary: The inverse problem of identifying spatially varying material properties of heterogeneous solids using experimentally available displacement fields and boundary reaction forces alone remains challenging. Being able to characterize heterogeneous and graded solids would be advantageous in the design and manufacturing of functionally graded materials and composites. Additionally, an efficient technique for identifying heterogeneous material properties from in vivo measurements would be useful in biomedical contexts to characterize heterogeneous biological tissues. Although several techniques developed over the past two decades have addressed inverse identification for homogeneous materials, including linear elastic, hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and elastoplastic solids, comparatively fewer studies have considered heterogeneous and graded materials. Furthermore, several recent approaches to characterizing heterogeneous and graded materials employ parameter-heavy, deep learning-based frameworks trained to enforce force equilibrium at specified collocation points within the material. In this work, we propose an interpretable and time-efficient framework that predicts the three-dimensional relative spatial variation of a constitutive parameter field for multiple parameters of a heterogeneous hyperelastic material, using only displacement-field data. In this work, we validate our framework on 3D synthetic and 2D experimental benchmarks involving heterogeneous, graded, and anisotropic hyperelastic materials. By leveraging the linear nature of the inverse problem for hyperelastic materials and directly optimizing for the constitutive parameters at the finite-element level, we achieve acceptable prediction accuracy with significantly lower computational time compared to recently reported deep-learning-based frameworks.

Machine Learning 1.title: Protecting Confidentiality, Privacy and Integrity in Collaborative Learning
Machine Learning 1.summary:
A collaboration between dataset owners and model owners is needed for effective machine learning (ML) training. During this collaboration, however, dataset owners and model owners want to protect the confidentiality of their respective assets (i.e., datasets, models and training code), with the dataset owners also caring about the privacy of individual users whose data is in the datasets. Existing solutions provide limited confidentiality for models and training code, suffer from data privacy issues, or incur unacceptable performance.
  We present Citadel++, a collaborative ML training system to simultaneously protect the confidentiality of datasets, models and training code as well as the privacy of individual user data. Specifically, Citadel++ takes a chained approach. First, we employ the Virtual Machine-level Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) as the training runtime to provide confidentiality protections for datasets, model and training code. Second, we create a privacy barrier that improves upon differential privacy techniques to safeguard the privacy of individual user data while maintaining model utility. Third, we construct and optimize a Virtual Machine Privilege Level (VMPL)-enforced fine-grained sandbox to regulate the dataflow in the system to ensure that our privacy barrier is always applied even when the model and training code maybe maliciously designed. Finally, we employ specific TEE capabilities to ensure the integrity of our privacy barrier and sandboxing mechanisms for their correct execution.
  To our knowledge, Citadel++ is the first collaborative training system providing strong confidentiality and privacy protections for dataset owners and model owners simultaneously. We analyze Citadel++ security properties and implement a full prototype. Our evaluation shows that Citadel++ provides strong guarantees with modest overheads.

Machine Learning 1.title: RAP: Radial-Angular Random Projection for Hyperbolic Representations
Machine Learning 1.summary: Random projection is a basic compression primitive for Euclidean representation learning, with the Johnson--Lindenstrauss lemma giving a target dimension $k=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log n)$ independent of the ambient dimension. As hyperbolic representations gain increasing attention in modern Transformers, vision-language models, and large language models, the same need for oblivious dimensionality reduction arises, but no analogous primitive yet exists for hyperbolic representations. We study this gap. Two natural attempts fail in dual ways: a tangent-space scheme gives a clean local guarantee but is chart-bound and pays a curvature penalty, while a fully hyperbolic projection in the hyperboloid model is geometrically native but mixes radial and angular error before feeding them into the conditioning of $\operatorname{arcosh}$. We propose radial-angular random projection (RAP), which preserves the radial coordinate exactly and applies a Euclidean random projection only to the angular direction, lifting the result back to the target hyperboloid. RAP is hyperbolic-to-hyperbolic by construction, costs one Gaussian matrix-vector product, and reduces hyperbolic compression to a normalized angular JL question on $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. We prove a finite-set RAP guarantee with explicit $\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_x)\sinh(\sqrt{c}\,r_y)$ conditioning, complemented by a local tangent-space JL theorem and an arcosh-conditioning lemma for the fully hyperbolic comparator. Across an origin-centered broad-radius point cloud, a balanced tree, a clustered Gaussian, and the WordNet noun hierarchy, RAP attains the lowest mean relative distortion in every $(n,k)$ cell, reducing distortion over the strongest hyperbolic baseline by approximately $48\%$--$49\%$ on broad-radius data. RAP also scales to million-point datasets and improves retrieval on vision--language representations over hyperbolic projection baselines.

Multimedia.title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
Multimedia.summary: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.

Multimedia.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
Multimedia.summary: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted at the 40th Pacific Asia Conference on Language, Information and Computation (PACLIC 40)

Multimedia.title: Beyond Code and Pixels: Co-Generating Editable and Visually Rich Presentations
Multimedia.summary: Generating PPTX presentations is a structured task that requires semantic planning, visual composition, precise layout, and editability, motivating collaboration among specialized agents. However, programmatic methods offer editability but often produce rigid designs, while image-based methods provide visual richness but flatten content into difficult-to-edit pixels. A hybrid system can combine these strengths, but must coordinate interdependent decisions across content, layout, and appearance. To address this challenge, we propose SlidesWeaver, a hybrid multi-agent system that coordinates language and vision agents through shared deck- and slide-level states. Specifically, it uses staged multimodal commitment, diffusion-based composition planning, and two generation schedules for different priorities between composition freedom and accurate text preservation, while preserving native text and geometry. Across 1,728 generations spanning 24 system-model configurations, SlidesWeaver achieves consistently superior overall quality across all evaluated dimensions while maintaining structural control, editability, and practical generation efficiency.

Multimedia.title: On Semiotic-Grounded Interpretive Evaluation of Generative Art
Multimedia.summary: Interpretation is essential to deciphering the language of art: audiences communicate with artists by recovering meaning from visual artifacts. However, current Generative Art (GenArt) evaluators primarily emphasize surface-level image quality or literal prompt adherence, failing to assess the deeper symbolic or contextual meaning intended by the creator. We formalize this observation using Peircean computational semiotic theory that models Human-GenArt Interaction (HGI) as cascaded semiosis. This framework reveals that artistic meaning is conveyed through iconic, symbolic, and indexical modes, whereas appearance-centered evaluators tend to emphasize the iconic mode. Building on this account, we propose SemJudge, an interpretation-centric evaluation framework that uses a Hierarchical Semiosis Graph (HSG) to reconstruct meaning conveyance from prompt to generated artifact. Experiments on an interpretation-intensive benchmark, SemiosisArt, show that SemJudge aligns more closely with human judgments than existing baselines. User studies further demonstrate that SemJudge produces deeper, more insightful artistic interpretations. We hope these findings pave the way for GenArt to move beyond the generation of "pretty" images toward a medium capable of understanding and expressing complex human experience. Project page: https://github.com/songrise/SemJudge
Multimedia.comment: ACM MM 2026

Multimedia.title: Hierarchical Semantic Learning for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Missing Modalities
Multimedia.summary: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) in real-world systems must handle unpredictable modality missingness caused by sensor failures, privacy masking, and unstable transmission. Existing methods either learn reliability-aware representations or reconstruct missing inputs, often using a single flattened encoder output. This overlooks deep encoders' semantic hierarchy and intra- and inter-modal interactions, causing semantic averaging and ill-posed mappings. We propose Hierarchical Semantic Learning (HSL), a framework that exploits semantic hierarchy for robust MSA with missing modalities. Hierarchical Semantic Decoupling exposes low-, mid-, and high-level feature streams from each modality encoder. Cross-Modal Cross-Level Semantic Reconstruction performs ladder-style recovery, using high-level semantics from observed modalities as global anchors to progressively reconstruct mid-level structures and low-level details of missing modalities. To stabilize cross-level reconstruction, Hierarchical Cascade Error Supervisor applies prototypical contrastive regularization to observed and reconstructed features, enforcing level-specific semantic consistency and limiting error propagation. Finally, Hierarchical Interactive Fusion captures dense interactions across modalities and semantic levels to produce robust predictions under diverse missingness patterns. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, IEMOCAP, and CH-SIMS show that HSL outperforms baselines in most missing-modality settings.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted for Publication in IEEE Transactions on Multimedia (TMM), 2026

Multimedia.title: Class Agnostic Instance-level Descriptor for Instance Search
Multimedia.summary: Despite the great success of the deep features in content-based image retrieval, the visual instance search remains challenging due to the lack of effective instance-level feature representation. Supervised or weakly supervised object detection methods are not the appropriate solutions due to their poor performance on the unknown object categories. In this paper, based on the feature set output from self-supervised ViT, the instance-level region discovery is modeled as detecting the compact feature subsets in a hierarchical fashion. The hierarchical decomposition results in a hierarchy of instance regions. On the one hand, this kind of hierarchical decomposition well addresses the problem of object embedding and occlusions, which are widely observed in real scenarios. On the other hand, the non-leaf nodes and leaf nodes on the hierarchy correspond to the instance regions in different granularities within an image. Therefore, features in uniform length are produced for these instance regions, which may cover across a dominant image region, an integral of multiple instances, or various individual instances. Such a collection of features allows us to unify the image retrieval, multi-instance search, and instance search into one framework. The empirical studies on three benchmarks show that such an instance-level descriptor remains effective on both the known and unknown object categories. Moreover, the superior performance is achieved on single-instance and multi-instance search, as well as image retrieval tasks.
Multimedia.comment: Added further evaluation on ILIAS Core with different detector and descriptor backbones

Multimedia.title: AVENUE: Audio-Video EditiNg Understanding and Evaluation
Multimedia.summary: Audio-video (AV) editing aims to modify audio and video content according to a target prompt. Unlike single-modality editing, AV editing requires models to infer a modality-selective edit scope from the prompt alone: determining not only what should change, but also which modality should be preserved. Faithfully evaluating such models therefore requires both (i) benchmarks that span diverse edit types and modality categories, and (ii) evaluation that is itself modality-aware and sample-specific. However, existing AV editing benchmarks provide limited coverage of edit types and modality combinations, while current evaluation systems are often modality-blind and sample-agnostic, making it difficult to assess whether models faithfully preserve the unintended modality. To address these gaps, we introduce AVENUE, Audio-Video EditiNg Understanding and Evaluation, comprising two contributions: (1) a benchmark of 1,291 source clips and 7,957 editing instructions across audio-targeted, video-targeted, and AV-coupled edit types, curated and human-verified from VGGSound; and (2) a sample-specific, modality-aware evaluation framework that specifies, for each sample, both the intended change and the content that must remain intact. We evaluate representative AV editing models spanning three editing paradigms : joint, sequential, and separate, providing the first systematic analysis of modality-selectivity across paradigms. Our findings reveal a fundamental open challenge: when editing one modality, existing models frequently induce unintended changes in the other, regardless of paradigm. AVENUE provides a benchmark and modality-aware evaluation framework to drive progress toward more controllable AV editing models. Our dataset is publicly available on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/datasets/AVENUE-dataset/AVENUE.
Multimedia.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track

Multimedia.title: PIRA: Pan-CDN Intra-video Resource Adaptation for Short Video Streaming
Multimedia.summary: In large scale short video platforms, CDN resource selection plays a critical role in maintaining Quality of Experience (QoE) while controlling escalating traffic costs. To better understand this phenomenon, we conduct in the wild network measurements during video playback in a production short video system. The results reveal that CDNs delivering higher average QoE often come at greater financial cost, yet their connection quality fluctuates even within a single video underscoring a fundamental and dynamic trade off between QoE and cost. However, the problem of sustaining high QoE under cost constraints remains insufficiently investigated in the context of CDN selection for short video streaming. To address this, we propose PIRA, a dynamic resource selection algorithm that optimizes QoE and cost in real time during video playback. PIRA formally integrating QoE and cost by a mathematical model, and introduce a intra video control theoretic CDN resource selection approach which can balance QoE and cost under network dynamics. To reduce the computation overheads, PIRA employs state space pruning and adaptive parameter adjustment to efficiently solve the high dimensional optimization problem. In large scale production experiments involving 450,000 users over two weeks, PIRA outperforms the production baseline, achieving a 2.1% reduction in start up delay, 15.2% shorter rebuffering time, and 10% lower average unit traffic cost, demonstrating its effectiveness in balancing user experience and financial cost at scale.

Multimedia.title: Learning Temporal Stabilization for Double-Talk-Robust Delay Estimation in Acoustic Echo Cancellation
Multimedia.summary: Acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) depends on accurate time-delay estimation (TDE): the adaptive canceller converges only after the bulk delay between the far-end reference and the microphone is compensated. GCC-PHAT remains the standard TDE front-end and, in our stress tests, wins or ties against a fully learned estimator under interference, low SNR, strong reverberation, loudspeaker nonlinearity, and noisy references. Its principal failure mode is short-window sustained double-talk, where near-end speech creates spurious correlation peaks that classical smoothing and confidence gating cannot reliably suppress. We therefore retain GCC-PHAT as a fixed, non-learnable backbone and learn only a 13.2K-parameter causal 2-D CNN stabilizer over the time--lag correlogram. The stabilizer exploits a simple temporal distinction: true delays form persistent ridges, whereas double-talk artifacts appear as transient spikes. Across synthetic and real AEC-Challenge echo paths, it reduces MAE and gross-outlier rates by approximately $3$--$5\x$ over tuned classical estimators and the WebRTC AEC3 matched filter. A faithful AEC3-style downstream testbed further shows that these delay gains translate into lower echo-leak rates and faster post-jump ERLE recovery in time-varying regimes, closing much of the gap to the oracle-delay ceiling. An optional coarse-to-fine pre-alignment stage extends the same residual stabilizer to stable 100--400\,ms bulk delays without retraining, while keeping the learned component focused on short-window double-talk robustness.

Machine Learning 2.title: Sliding-Window Detection of Hidden Regimes under Stochastic Switching
Machine Learning 2.summary: A sliding-window average is a simple estimator of the current state of a hidden regime-switching process, such as a hidden Markov model. A longer window averages out more noise but is more likely to contain a switch, and the question is what such a switch costs. We analyse the decoder that assigns the average of the last $m$ observations to the nearest regime mean. For two regimes with conditionally independent, stochastically ordered observations, a switch inside the window, averaged uniformly over its positions and directions, causes an error with probability exactly $1/2$. Consequently, for every stationary switching law, the error is at most $\bar P(m)+\bar s(m-1)/2$, where $\bar P(m)$ is the stationary-weighted single-regime error and $\bar s$ the switch rate. Under Markov switching, time reversal shows that a window whose oldest and current regimes differ is misclassified with probability exactly $1/2$, however many switches it contains, and the bound is attained up to a factor $p_{\min}^{m-1}$. For Gaussian noise with common variance, minimizing the bound gives an explicit window length which, in units of $σ^2/Δ^2$, depends only on the expected number of switches in that time. As switching probabilities vanish proportionally, the optimal error is $\bar s\log(1/\bar s)/(2I)(1+o(1))$, with $I$ the single-regime Chernoff exponent. In the Gaussian case this is twice the Bayes error. For symmetric switching, exponentially weighted moving averages reduce this factor to at most $2\log2\approx1.39$, and two-block weights adapted to the switch rate attain the Bayes rate. For three or more regimes, long-window switch costs are set by the geometry of the regime means. For Markov-modulated random walks with $\pm1$ steps on a reflecting lattice, a position-aware decoder learns as fast as without walls under holding boundaries, while steps at bouncing boundaries carry none.
Machine Learning 2.comment: 29 pages, 8 figures. Code and data: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24532266

Machine Learning 2.title: The Look-Elsewhere Effect in Searches for New Physics: from Classical Methods to Machine Learning
Machine Learning 2.summary: The look-elsewhere effect (LEE) arises when the location of an effect in parameter space is not specified in advance: scanning many locations inflates the significance of the largest excess, and the local $p$-value must be corrected into a global one. A well-established framework, rooted in the work of Davies and operationalised for particle physics by Gross and Vitells, provides this correction for scans over continuous parameters. Some aspects, however, remain unsettled. The definition of "elsewhere" is ambiguous and ranges from a single distribution to an entire experimental programme. Moreover, the analytical shortcuts of the classical framework do not carry over to searches based on machine learning (ML), which are affected by an implicit post-selection bias that depends on the model's resolution and expressiveness. This review covers the LEE in searches for new physics at colliders, from its statistical foundations to these modern challenges. We discuss the corrections for continuous scans and for multiple discrete tests, illustrated with simple numerical examples, and the interaction between ML and the LEE, which we connect to the broader literature on selective inference. We highlight open problems, including the computational cost of empirical calibration for complex models and the development of analytical shortcuts for ML test statistics, and offer recommendations for reporting discovery significance in both classical and ML-based searches in particle physics.

Machine Learning 2.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $β\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($β>0$) and risk-seeking ($β<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|β|/(1-γ)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.

Machine Learning 2.title: Conditional Independence Graph Learning from Dependent Data Via Time-Delay Embedding
Machine Learning 2.summary: We consider the problem of inferring the conditional independence graph (CIG) of a high-dimensional stationary multivariate Gaussian time series which could be short-range dependent (SRD) or long-range dependent (LRD). In a time series graph, each component of the vector series is represented by a distinct node, and associations between components are represented by edges between the corresponding nodes. We consider a time-domain approach based on time-delay embedding, casting the problem as one of multi-attribute graph estimation for random vectors where a vector is associated with each node of the graph. For an embedding dimension $d$, at each node the associated $(d+1)$-dimensional random vector consists of a time series component and its $d$ delayed copies, with integer delays up to $d \ge 1$. Graph estimation from dependent data has been investigated in the past using frequency-domain methods whose analysis is restricted to SRD data. We consider a penalized negative pseudo log-likelihood function with convex lasso or non-convex regularizations to estimate the CIG. Non-convex regularization functions are log-sum, smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) and minimax concave penalty (MCP). We exploit an existing alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) approach to optimize the objective function. We establish sufficient conditions in a high-dimensional setting for consistency, local convexity when using non-convex penalties, and graph recovery, for both SRD and LRD series. We illustrate our approach with both synthetic and real-data examples. For a $p$-dimensional time series, the computational complexity of the ADMM algorithm is ${\cal O}((d+1)^3 p^3)$. Based on the numerical examples, a heuristic is suggested and illustrated for selection of $d$ which, in theory, should tend to infinity to infer the time series graph.

Machine Learning 2.title: Global Convergence of Second-Order Methods for Physics-Informed Neural Networks in the Overparameterized Limit
Machine Learning 2.summary: Solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) constitutes a core task in many engineering and scientific disciplines. Physics-informed neural networks and the deep Galerkin method effectively leverage machine learning models to approximate solutions of known PDEs by minimizing residuals corresponding to the PDE operator alongside external constraints. Although second-order optimizers are becoming increasingly popular for training neural networks (NNs) to solve PDEs and empirically outperform their first-order counterparts in both speed and accuracy, the convergence theory for training such models is essentially confined to first-order methods. In this paper, we close this gap and develop a convergence analysis for the regularized Newton and Gauss-Newton methods. As the number of hidden units tends to infinity, the training dynamics converge in probability, with explicit rates, to the solution of a deterministic limit equation involving a Newton neural tangent kernel operator associated with the PDE. Although the limiting kernel operator admits no spectral gap, we prove that, in the overparameterized limit, the PDE residual vanishes as training proceeds, and, under mild assumptions, the NN converges to the PDE solution. We further show that, provided a sufficiently small regularization parameter, the projection of the residual onto any fixed number of leading eigenfunctions decays exponentially fast, demonstrating that this hyperparameter acts as a spectral filter: it lifts the convergence rates of high-frequency components toward those of low-frequency ones, thereby mitigating the spectral bias inherent in gradient descent. Mathematical challenges arise from the implicit parameter update involving a linear system whose dimension increases with the NN width and, for Newton's method, a potentially indefinite Hessian, as well as from the PDE operator entering the kernel.

Machine Learning 2.title: Guiding Multi-Objective Genetic Programming with Description Length Improves Symbolic Regression Solutions
Machine Learning 2.summary: Symbolic regression with genetic programming (GPSR) may suffer from overfitting and structural bloat, especially when noise is present. In this paper we evaluate description length (DL) and fractional Bayes factor (FBF) criteria as principled, data-efficient alternatives to heuristics for selecting compact expressions that generalise well. We implement DL using a Fisher-information-based parameter encoding and compare it to the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) across multiple datasets, including noisy synthetic benchmarks and real-world regression problems. We study three search/selection strategies: (i) multi-objective search for accuracy and program length followed by DL/FBF selection; (ii) multi-objective search using DL directly as an objective; and (iii) single-objective optimisation with DL/FBF as the fitness. Across datasets, we find that DL/FBF post-selection improves test performance compared to AIC/BIC baseline and that BIC in combination with the same function complexity penalty from DL/FBF produces similar results. In contrast, using DL/FBF directly as a fitness function in single-objective GPSR frequently induces premature convergence to overly simple models. We conclude with practical guidance for using DL/FBF as robust model-selection tools in genetic programming workflows.

Machine Learning 2.title: Compatible Likelihoods for Flow Matching on Manifolds
Machine Learning 2.summary: On the simplest non-Euclidean manifold, the 1D flat torus, we exhibit a distribution where a recent extension of Riemannian flow matching is globally optimized by a velocity field that pushes samples away from the data distribution. We trace this failure mode to a property we call compatibility; a likelihood-based flow matching objective is compatible if its population minimizer recovers the marginal velocity field induced by the data and coupling. We derive a general condition for compatibility, apply it to existing methods, and bound the worst-case error by a residual term that vanishes under compatibility. On compact manifolds, we show that existing compatible objectives put density on infeasible velocities. To tackle both issues, we propose an exponential family over endpoints with the conditional velocity as sufficient statistic, which is both compatible and supported only on feasible velocities. In practice, and with low overhead, this reduces to a reweighting of the flow matching loss. On spaces of constant curvature, this treats errors in flow speed and direction differently. Compared to prior art, our method finds the correct velocities on the test case, outperforms in general on high-dimensional product tori, and, for two of four standard geospatial benchmarks on the sphere, achieves substantial NLL improvements. When evaluated on a large dataset of human poses, our method surpasses prior work according to sample-based metrics.
Machine Learning 2.comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)

Machine Learning 2.title: Fixed Points and Envelope Dynamics on Credal Hyperspaces
Machine Learning 2.summary: Let $X$ be a compact metric space and consider the hyperspace $\mathscr C_X$ of nonempty weakly closed convex sets of Borel probability measures on $X$, called credal sets. These sets represent uncertainty about which probability law governs the phenomenon of interest. We equip $\mathscr C_X$ with the Hausdorff metric induced by a metric for weak convergence. Credal order intervals $[\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B}] = \{ \mathcal{P}\in\mathscr C_X: \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{B} \}$ are complete lattices, and every inclusion-monotone, Hausdorff-continuous self map of such an interval has least and greatest fixed points obtained as limits of iteration from $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$. For families of inclusion-monotone updates that may vary with time, we construct lower and upper envelope maps that bound every admissible trajectory. When these envelope maps are Hausdorff-continuous, the distance of every trajectory from a limiting credal interval vanishes uniformly over all switching sequences and initial credal sets. Coalescence of the limiting interval endpoints yields convergence to a common credal limit. We then construct the credal evolution induced by a time consistent Nisio semigroup. Uniform $W_1$ contraction of the underlying Markov semigroups induces Hausdorff-Wasserstein contraction of the credal evolution, yielding a unique common invariant credal set, exponential convergence from every initial credal set, and a support functional equal to the robust ergodic limit. We also derive perturbation bounds from finite time Nisio discrepancies and one step kernel set discrepancies, and characterize the countable sequences of support coordinates that represent credal sets, providing an explicit reconstruction formula.

Machine Learning 2.title: Out-of-the-Box Tabular Foundation Models for Bayesian Optimization in Materials Discovery
Machine Learning 2.summary: Bayesian optimization is widely used in active learning loops for materials science. Gaussian processes serve as the de-facto surrogate model family, but require task-dependent kernel choices and can lack the modeling capacity for complex relationships. Tabular foundation models (TFMs) have recently emerged as the state-of-the-art for predictive tasks on structured data, without requiring bespoke kernels or hyperparameter tuning. We evaluate two TFMs, TabPFN and TabICL, as out-of-the-box surrogate models on two standard materials science benchmarks, comparing against a large field of baselines encompassing Gaussian processes, random forests, and CatBoost. Our findings indicate that TFMs are highly competitive surrogate models across the two benchmarks, without task-specific training for active learning or GP kernel selection. Our results motivate developing TFMs further as surrogates for active learning in materials discovery.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Accepted at the AI4Mat Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 19 pages, 12 figures, 5 tables. Code: https://github.com/PriorLabs/matsci-bo-bench

Machine Learning 2.title: Local structural transfer learning of non-Gaussian DAG and its application to multi-source cancer gene regulatory networks
Machine Learning 2.summary: Directed acyclic graph (DAG) is pivotal for modeling gene regulatory networks in cancer pathogenesis, yet single-study genomic data is often limited for accurate DAG reconstruction. Although multi-source datasets provide augmented sample sizes, substantial heterogeneity persists across real-world cohorts. It remains an open question how to pool the heterogeneous data with only local similarity together for better DAG structure reconstruction in the target study. In this paper, we introduce a novel set of structural similarity measures for DAGs and then present a transfer DAG learning framework by effectively leveraging information from auxiliary DAGs with node-level local similarities. Our theoretical analysis shows substantial improvement in terms of DAG reconstruction in the target study, which is in sharp contrast to most existing transfer learning methods requiring global similarity. The advantage of the proposed transfer DAG learning is also supported by extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic data and multi-source cancer genomics data.

Machine Learning 2.title: Change Point Detection with Generative Models
Machine Learning 2.summary: Change point detection (CPD) methods aim to identify abrupt changes in the properties of time series, which is a key problem in numerous fields. A major class of CPD approaches relies on computing a CPD score, which is either a discrepancy or divergence between two subsequent samples, called windows. A fundamental limitation of window-based CPD is the 'sample size bottleneck.' To ensure temporal precision, windows must be small; however, small samples provide insufficient statistical evidence for the classifiers and deep-learning models currently used to compute CPD scores. This leads to high variance in the scores and frequent mispredictions. Our study tackles this issue by exploring generative models for window augmentation, effectively expanding available data to improve CPD quality. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly enhances CPD. Specifically, we show that this approach allows simple classifiers to outperform complex deep-learning baselines by stabilizing the CPD score distribution.

Machine Learning 2.title: Statistical Inference for Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent
Machine Learning 2.summary: Privacy preservation in machine learning, particularly through Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD), is crucial for analyzing sensitive data. However, existing statistical inference methods for SGD predominantly focus on cyclic subsampling, while DP-SGD requires randomized subsampling. This paper first bridges this gap by establishing the asymptotic properties of SGD under the randomized rule and extending these results to DP-SGD. For DP-SGD, we show that the asymptotic variance decomposes into statistical, sampling, and privacy-induced components. We propose two methods for constructing valid confidence intervals: the plug-in method and the random scaling method. We also perform extensive numerical analysis showing that the proposed confidence intervals achieve nominal coverage rates while maintaining privacy.

Machine Learning 2.title: Stability Regularized Cross-Validation
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study hyperparameter selection via cross-validation, motivated by settings in which the selected $k$-fold cross-validation error underestimates the selected model's test error. We propose a nested $k$-fold cross-validation scheme that minimizes a weighted sum of the standard cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, with the stability weight selected by an outer cross-validation loop. We derive a generalization bound that controls test error using the cross-validation error and empirical hypothesis stability, together with correction terms common to every candidate. In a stylized ridge regression setting, we then show that whether the stability weight improves expected test-set performance depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, with the greatest improvement when the signal-to-noise ratio is small. On $13$ real-world regression datasets, the procedure reduces the average out-of-sample MSE relative to $k$-fold cross-validation by $5.6\%$ for sparse regression and by $6.8\%$ for CART. A side benefit of an outer cross-validation loop is that the selected error estimates are better calibrated than those from ordinary $k$-fold cross-validation: the error estimate moves from 12.3\% below the selected test-set MSE to 5.8\% above it for sparse regression and from 10.3\% below to 0.2\% above it for CART.

Machine Learning 2.title: Cell-Type-Specific Expression Is Hard to Predict from Bulk, but It Is Still Useful
Machine Learning 2.summary: Single-cell-informed deconvolution provides cell-type-resolved features for clinical bulk RNA cohorts. Most existing methods predict the proportions $π_k$ of the $K$ constituent cell types (CTs). Fewer predict cell-type-specific expression (CTSE) $μ_{kg}$ of gene $g$ in CT $k$, which can capture cell states that proportions miss, but recent benchmarks find it much harder. We explain this gap with closed-form accuracy bounds. For CTSE, we derive an $R^2$ ceiling for per-gene linear estimators. For proportions, the best linear estimator, which pools evidence across genes, has a closed-form $R^2$, and a computable lower bound on it predicts which CTs are learnable. We study targeted deconvolution of 106 biologically curated (CT, gene) pairs, found post hoc to have higher learnability scores. On overall survival in non-small cell lung cancer, estimation difficulty does not predict prognostic value across these targets. Yet a sparse survival model on deconvolved features, mostly CTSE, predicts survival as well as a sparse model on the bulk genes themselves, while attributing its signal to specific cell types. Some deconvolved CTSE features reveal prognostic signal not seen in the corresponding bulk gene.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Drug Discovery (AI4DD). 5 pages main text, 28 pages total

Machine Learning 2.title: Accelerated Proximal Gradient Methods for Multiobjective Optimization over Probability Measures via Hilbert-Space Lifting
Machine Learning 2.summary: Many sampling and inference tasks require a single distribution that balances several targets. We formulate this task as multiobjective optimization of Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergences over probability measures, in the Pareto sense. The particle method MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2025) uses explicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version A-MWGraD (Nguyen et al., 2026) lacks discrete-time guarantees. We propose the multiobjective Wasserstein proximal gradient (MWPG), which uses implicit Wasserstein gradient steps, and its accelerated version, multiobjective Wasserstein accelerated proximal gradient (MWAPG), with rigorous discrete-time guarantees. Our key idea is a Hilbert-space lifting: each measure is represented as the pushforward of a fixed base measure by a map in a Hilbert space. The problem then becomes a constrained multiobjective composite problem over transport maps, to which accelerated proximal gradient methods apply. For convex and smooth potentials, we show that MWAPG decreases a Pareto merit function at the rate $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$; for $m$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth potentials, the rate is $\mathcal{O}\big((1-\sqrt{m/L})^k\big)$. We also give closed-form Gaussian updates and particle implementations based on input-convex neural networks, which require no score estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world dataset show that MWAPG needs far fewer iterations than MWPG and matches or outperforms A-MWGraD in Bayesian multi-task learning.

Machine Learning 2.title: Federated Community Detection in Bipartite Networks
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study federated spectral estimation when a large matrix is horizontally partitioned across servers that cannot share raw data. We propose FLICKER, a target-specific gradient-based power iteration that recovers a singular direction associated with a prescribed spectral target using only matrix-vector products on local blocks. Different target directions can be recovered independently and in parallel. We establish non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and provide a recursive grid-search procedure for spectral target selection. Building on FLICKER, we develop BiFLICKER for federated community detection in bipartite networks, together with a sequential projected variant for nearby or repeated singular directions. Under a sparse bipartite stochastic block model, we show that properly rescaled leading singular values from a reference server provide valid global targets, and that Sequential BiFLICKER achieves a vanishing misclustering rate and exact recovery under stronger sparsity conditions. Simulations show that BiFLICKER remains close to centralized spectral clustering and is more robust than existing federated spectral baselines when local sample sizes are small. On a LastFM user-artist network naturally partitioned by country, Sequential BiFLICKER attains an overall ARI of 0.96 against centralized clustering while revealing cross-country communities with distinct listening profiles.

Machine Learning 2.title: Asymptotically Efficient Finite Impulse Response System Identification without Noise Knowledge
Machine Learning 2.summary: Efficient identification of finite impulse response systems under unknown or heavy-tailed noise remains a challenge in system identification. Classical estimators, including least squares (LS) and robust alternatives like least absolute deviations (LAD), are often sensitive to outliers or statistically inefficient when noise characteristics deviate from their underlying assumptions. To address this, we propose a novel class of adaptive estimators that achieves asymptotic efficiency without requiring prior knowledge of the noise distribution. Our approach leverages kernel density estimation to construct two nonparametric maximum likelihood-type estimators: the estimated maximum likelihood estimator (eMLE) and the estimated profiled MLE (epMLE). These estimators approximate the likelihood using residuals from consistent initial estimates, avoiding parametric assumptions on the noise. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that, under mild regularity conditions, both eMLE and epMLE are consistent, asymptotically normal, and attain the Cramér--Rao lower bound, thereby achieving asymptotic efficiency. Additionally, we develop computationally efficient one-step Newton--Raphson algorithms that implement these estimators without sacrificing asymptotic efficiency. Extensive simulations across various noise distributions confirm that the proposed methods outperform classical LS and LAD estimators in both robustness and accuracy, often matching oracle MLE performance.

Machine Learning 2.title: High-Order Gaussian Approximation of Besov Functions on Manifolds
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study high-order Gaussian approximation for Besov functions $f\in B^α_{2,\infty}(X)$ with $α>0$ on a compact smooth embedded manifold $X$ without boundary. For $r<α$, a suitable signed combination of Gaussian integral operators at different bandwidths gives an $H^r(X)$ error bounded by $Cγ^{α-r}\|f\|_{B^α_{2,\infty}(X)}$. The squared Gaussian RKHS norm of the approximant is bounded by $Cγ^{-\varrho}\|f\|_{L_2(X)}^2$, where $\varrho$ is the intrinsic dimension of $X$. We apply these approximation results to two statistical learning problems. For regularized Gaussian logistic classification, we combine the approximation bounds with a localized oracle inequality. For a potentially unbounded Bayes function in $B^α_{2,\infty}(X)$ and a marginal density in $L_p(X)$, the excess logistic risk has upper bounds of order $((\log n)^{\varrho+1}/n)^{2β/(2β+3\varrho)}$ for the unclipped predictor and $((\log n)^{\varrho+2}/n)^{β/(β+\varrho)}$ for clipped predictions with suitably selected parameters, where $β=2α(1-1/p)$. Under bounded marginal densities, our excess misclassification risk bound matches, up to logarithmic factors, the classical Hölder-class exponent. For elliptic operator learning, we assemble a Gaussian Galerkin solution operator from random manifold samples. Its error in the operator norm from $B^α_{2,\infty}(X)$ to $H^1(X)$ is bounded with high probability by two terms. The trial-space term has a decay exponent in the number of Gaussian centers that can approach $(α+1)/\varrho$. The bias and sampling term is of order $n^{-2N/(4N+\varrho)}$ for a fixed trial space, where $n$ is the number of sample pairs and $N$ is the number of Gaussian scales used for matrix assembly. The convergence rates for both problems depend on the intrinsic dimension $\varrho$ and are independent of the ambient dimension $d$.

Machine Learning 2.title: BReD: Block Replay Dithering for Stable Low-Bit EMA Optimizer States
Machine Learning 2.summary: Low-bit storage of optimizer states can substantially reduce the memory footprint of large-scale training. In practice, however, these states are not quantized once: at every training step, they are dequantized, updated, requantized, and written back. This iterative quantization pipeline can destabilize training. We identify a failure mode behind this instability: for states updated via exponential moving averages (EMAs), quantization errors are recursively fed into subsequent updates. As a result, biased errors accumulate over time while high-variance errors are amplified, particularly when the EMA decay factor is close to 1. To address this error accumulation, we propose BReD (Block Replay Dithering), a method that reduces rounding bias and controls rounding variance during quantization. BReD adapts classical subtractive dithering to optimizer-state quantization by combining deterministic seed replay with block-wise shared dither values, avoiding auxiliary random-tensor storage and per-element dither values generation. Across the default pretraining settings (five optimizers at 120M; AdamW and Muon at 1.1B and 3.4B model) and supervised fine-tuning (AdamW and Muon at 7B model), 4-bit BReD closely matches training with full-precision optimizer states, with PPL shifts $\leq0.5$ in pretraining and $\leq0.2$ in fine-tuning and average downstream performance changes within 0.7 points. Moreover, 3-bit BReD preserves stable convergence in the evaluated settings, offering a more aggressive alternative. Our implementation of BReD is available at: https://github.com/ZhanHeshen/BReD

Machine Learning 2.title: A Graphical Criterion for Linear Causal Bounds
Machine Learning 2.summary: The values of causal effects and counterfactuals are typically only partially identified from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding. With discretely-valued variables, under certain conditions, sharp bounds can be derived by solving one linear program. This is then computationally tractable for many causal questions. In this paper, for every diagram in which each confounded component has at most two hidden causes, we give necessary and sufficient conditions for the sharp bounds to be equal to the optimum of one linear program for every (positive) input probability table. This algorithm is implemented in a new Python package, called "partialid", that allows users to compose assumptions, queries, and data to obtain sharp bounds in a computationally tractable manner.

Machine Learning 2.title: CondUQ: Calibrated Conditional Uncertainty Quantification Using Distribution Matching
Machine Learning 2.summary: Many applications, especially reliability- and safety-critical ones, require accurate uncertainty quantification for the outputs of model- or learning-based measurement, estimation, and prediction systems. The errors of such systems often vary with factors such as input quality and operating conditions, and thus cannot be accurately described by a single Gaussian model. Although Gaussian mixture models and calibrated quantiles can approximate such error distributions, their unconditional forms do not capture how the error behavior depends on these factors. Hence, we propose condUQ, an approach that conditions error models on observable factors for enabling accurate and reliable uncertainty quantification. condUQ is built on top of an existing system without modifying it and applies even when the system is a black box. First, condUQ maps the observable factors to a latent quality index (QI) such that errors sharing the same QI follow a common, approximately Gaussian conditional distribution. The QI predictor is trained end-to-end with a distribution-matching objective, without requiring quality labels. Second, for each QI, a Gaussian error model is then fitted and calibrated on a large held-out dataset. condUQ is demonstrated on three examples: (a) GPS multipath errors conditioned on satellite elevation and signal strength, (b) relative attitude errors of a transformer-based visual relative pose regression model conditioned on its internal features of the image pairs, and (c) prediction errors of a world model conditioned on the input observations and actions. In all three examples, condUQ substantially reduces the discrepancy between the modeled and empirical error distributions compared with a single global model. Moreover, the learned QIs reveal how the underlying factors affect the error characteristics in a manner consistent with physical principles.

Machine Learning 2.title: Extreme Binary Classification: Extreme Value Theory for Extreme Constraint on False Negative
Machine Learning 2.summary:
While binary classification is one of the most extensively studied problems in machine learning,
  the regime in which the goal is to learn a classifier with an almost zero false negative rate remains largely unexplored.
  In this paper, we introduce the Extreme Binary Classification problem, where the objective is to learn a classifier whose false negative rate $α$ is constrained by $ε_{N_1}=o_{N_1\to\infty}(1/N_1)$, with $N_1$ denoting the number of positive examples in the training set.
  To address this problem, we propose a threshold adaptation method theoretically grounded in guarantees derived from Extreme Value Theory, together with a feature selection procedure based on a permutation test applied to sample maxima.
  Experimental results on four real-world datasets of varying sizes demonstrate that our approach compares favorably with state-of-the-art methods.
  In addition, we illustrate its interpretability through an application to a cancer screening dataset.

Machine Learning 2.title: Correlation-Aware Evidential Fusion for Trusted Multi-View Classification
Machine Learning 2.summary: Trusted multi-view classification aims to make accurate and reliable predictions by integrating information from multiple views. Existing methods typically estimate class evidence and uncertainty for each view and combine the resulting opinions through aggregation rules. However, they generally treat different views as independent information sources, overlooking the correlations among them. Highly correlated views tend to produce similar evidence, and treating them as independent sources may repeatedly count consistent information and give it disproportionate influence, while weakening complementary evidence that provides additional information. Consequently, such correlation-unaware fusion may not only limit classification performance but also produce miscalibrated uncertainty estimates. To address this issue, we propose Correlation-Aware Fusion of Evidence (CAFE), a framework for trusted multi-view classification. CAFE applies complementarity-based trust discounting to the evidence produced by view-private experts and introduces a correlation-aware constraint to reduce the repeated contribution of similar evidence. It then learns sample-specific weights from the global multi-view context to adaptively combine the correlation-adjusted private evidence with cross-view collaborative evidence. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that CAFE consistently improves classification and calibration performance in general settings, with particularly significant gains when strong correlations exist among views.

Machine Learning 2.title: Certifying a Sufficient Gaussian Dependence Regime for Learned Weighted FDR Control
Machine Learning 2.summary: Learning hypothesis weights from informative auxiliary data can improve the power of multiple testing. Even when the weights are learned independently of the tests, the validity of weighted Benjamini-Hochberg depends on their joint distribution. We use reference observations to certify a sufficient dependence condition for one-sided Gaussian tests. An intersection-union test of uncertain correlation signs determines whether to apply weighted Benjamini-Hochberg or a prespecified fallback at an adjusted level. Under conditional separation of certification and testing, the procedure controls the false discovery rate (FDR) for every Gaussian correlation matrix satisfying the stated sampling assumptions and weight constraints. We establish a boundary obstruction to uniform certification and matching minimax sample-size bounds for worst-case pair sets and the all-pairs problem. In the parameter ranges of the matching bounds, the minimax sample size grows logarithmically with the number of checked pairs and quadratically with the inverse of their positive margin. For homogeneous Gaussian observations with known marginal variances, residual contrasts from the testing subjects provide an independent source of certification scores. Simulations with up to 4,950 checked pairs, comparisons under a common subject budget, and Gaussian designs based on correlations estimated from the Healthy Brain Network illustrate the trade-off between certification and detection power.

Machine Learning 2.title: Minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap of continuous Markov chains, with applications to empirical concentration bounds
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study the minimax estimation of the pseudo-spectral gap $γ_{ps}$ of a Markov chain from the observation of a single trajectory. Extending earlier works on finite-state space chains by Wolfer and Kontorovich (2024), we provide an estimator in the case of a compact, continuous state-space. Our estimator appears to be minimax-optimal on the class of chains with a transition operator with Lipschitz density, up to logarithmic terms. Our estimator, combined with Paulin's version of Bernstein inequality, allows to derive empirical concentration inequalities for Markov chains. This unlocks many applications, from confidence intervals, to active learning and generalization bounds. In particular, for rested bandits with Markov rewards, we provide a version of UCB with a regret bound similar to the one in the iid case, without assuming any knowledge on the pseudo-spectral gap of the chains.

Machine Learning 2.title: Online Non-Monotone DR-Submodular Maximization Beyond $1/e$ with Feasible Gradient Queries
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study adversarial online maximization of nonnegative, non-monotone DR-submodular functions over compact convex down-closed sets $K\subseteq[0,1]^d$ when gradients may be queried only at feasible points. The online approximation coefficients $4/9$ (Aggarwal and Lu) and $2\sqrt{3}-3\approx 0.4641$ (Aggarwal and Du) rely on queries along chains that start from the all-ones vector and leave $K$. With every query in $K$, the best known coefficient was $1/e$. We give an online algorithm with coefficient $0.4013$ that, in each round, plays a random action, queries one gradient at a point of $K$, and makes one projection. Its expected approximate regret is $O(RB(1+R)\sqrt{T})$, where $R\le\sqrt{d}$ bounds the norm of points of $K$ and $B$ bounds the gradient norm on $K$. For a budget $\sum_i x_i\le k$, the bound is $O(kB\sqrt{T})$. The algorithm keeps a state $x\in K$, and the analysis applies the coordinate-chain comparison of Aggarwal and Lu inside the box $[0,x]$, which keeps every query feasible. A second comparison, along a path from $0$ in the direction $x$, cancels the extra terms that the box creates. Because the queries are feasible, they can be played, which gives regret $O(T^{2/3})$ under semi-bandit feedback and $O(T^{4/5})$ under bandit feedback with bounded values. Unbiased stochastic gradients with bounded second moment keep the $\sqrt{T}$ rate, and on a fixed function the algorithm attains $0.4013\,\mathrm{OPT}-\varepsilon$ in expectation with $O(1+R^2(1+R)^2B^2/\varepsilon^2)$ feasible gradient queries.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Completely rewritten: new approach and results

Machine Learning 2.title: Conformal Prediction and Conditional Coverage for Tabular Foundation Models
Machine Learning 2.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) provide predictive distributions for regression, but their prediction regions can exhibit undercoverage or overcoverage even when point predictions are accurate. We introduce C-USIM (Conditionally-Uniformized Score Integration Method), a lightweight application of highest predictive density split conformal prediction that accommodates multimodal predictions. Given calibration and test outputs, it requires no additional training or model inference. It provides finite-sample marginal validity under our assumptions. We bound conditional-marginal coverage gaps using distribution-estimation error and score discreteness, and examine coverage heterogeneity through percentile rank-score plots. Experiments with TabPFN and TabICL show improved marginal coverage accuracy and lower average conditional and group coverage errors. Under a fixed data budget, allocating more observations to calibration can reduce marginal coverage error despite less accurate point predictions.

Machine Learning 2.title: RHOPE: LLM-Augmented Adaptive Experimental Design with Complex Contextual Information
Machine Learning 2.summary: Experimental design allocates limited measurement effort across candidate treatments to learn their expected outcomes. Adaptive designs refine allocations as evidence accumulates, improving estimation and treatment selection. Contextual information can inform these decisions, but exploiting unstructured or high-dimensional context remains challenging. We use large language models (LLMs) to transform complex context into proxy outcomes and propose Residual Horizon Optimization for Prediction-Powered Experimentation (RHOPE), a principled Bayesian adaptive experimentation framework that combines true outcomes with LLM-generated proxy outcomes and formulates finite-batch design as a posterior Markov decision process (MDP). Our methodology uses proxy outcomes in two ways: sample augmentation improves estimation precision, while observing proxies before each allocation decision provides advance information. Synthetic experiments and semi-synthetic experiments using Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC) data suggest that estimation precision drives most gains, with smaller advance-information gains, and highlight the importance of proxy informativeness and moment-estimation accuracy.

Machine Learning 2.title: Understanding Double Descent through Universal Compression
Machine Learning 2.summary: Many deep learning models exhibit a double-descent phenomenon, where test loss exhibits a sharp peak near the interpolation threshold and then descends a second time as model size grows further, contrary to the U-shape predicted by the classical bias--variance tradeoff. The double-descent phenomenon has been found and explained in toy classical models, but is not well-understood in modern deep learning despite extensive empirical study. We interpret double descent through the novel lens of universal compression.
