Specifically, we upper bound the maximum-likelihood excess test loss as a sum of four terms: an approximation-and-shift term, a minimax batch regret, a prior cost, and an MLE-vs-Bayes gap. Under exact posterior sampling, we further show that the expected MLE-vs-ensemble gap lower-bounds the MLE-vs-Bayes gap in the well-specified setting. In our experiments, a Gaussian-prior SGLD approximation to the Bayes predictor, unlike SGD, shows no pronounced interpolation peak. Experiments with uniform random labels support this gap as a major contributor to the double-descent peak; here, the SGD cross-entropy is roughly four times the SGLD ensemble cross-entropy at the peak, while the ensemble cross-entropy remains near $\log 10$.

Machine Learning 2.title: Learning to Infer: Statistical Inference through Meta Learning
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study meta learning for statistical inference, in which neural networks learn inference rules from simulated tasks and apply them to new datasets without parameter updates, providing a form of in-context learning. We draw on statistical decision theory to design training objectives whose population minimizers are Bayes rules and exploit their connections to classical inference procedures to establish frequentist guarantees for the learned rules. The structure of classical inference procedures also motivates the design of our neural network architecture, called Residual Recurrent Deep Sets (RRDS), which repeatedly aggregates information across observations in a permutation-invariant manner and refines its internal state through residual updates. Under suitable regularity and training conditions, we establish asymptotic efficiency in parameter estimation, consistency in model selection, and variable selection guarantees in high-dimensional regression models. The RRDS architecture allows us to avoid the curse of sample size that arises in generic neural network approximation when the network takes the entire dataset as input. For fixed-dimensional models, the network size and the number of meta training tasks need only grow polynomially in the sample size; under additional analyticity conditions, these requirements improve to polylogarithmic growth in network size and nearly linear growth in the number of training tasks. Numerical experiments illustrate the finite-sample advantages of the learned inference rules over classical methods.

Machine Learning 2.title: Debiased Inference via Posterior Corrections for High-Dimensional Regression
Machine Learning 2.summary: There has been significant progress in Bayesian inference based on sparsity-inducing priors, such as spike-and-slab and horseshoe priors, for high-dimensional regression. The resulting posteriors, however, in general do not possess desirable frequentist properties, and the credible sets thus cannot serve as valid confidence sets even asymptotically. We introduce a novel debiasing approach that corrects the bias for the entire (possibly approximate) Bayesian posterior distribution. We establish new Bernstein-von Mises theorems that guarantee the frequentist validity of the debiased law. We demonstrate the practical performance of our proposal through Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications in economics.

Machine Learning 2.title: How Many Sources, Not Just How Many Problems: Planning the Precision of LLM Evaluations from Earlier Results
Machine Learning 2.summary: When benchmark problems share sources, such as variants of one template or tasks from one repository, an evaluation budget must fix the number of sources as well as the number of problems. We ask whether pilot data or earlier evaluation results can predict, before an evaluation is run, how much the standard deviation (SD) of the score grows when the same budget is concentrated on fewer sources. We use the classical design effect with an intraclass correlation estimated on data disjoint from those used to check the prediction. On GSM-Symbolic, 100 problems drawn as 10 templates x 10 variants have an SD of 9.2 pp against 2.7 pp from 100 templates; pilot data on 15 other questions predict the ratio as 3.49 against 3.52 measured on held-out questions (medians over 20 splits; single splits err by -13% to +16%), once the actual sampling plan is included. On SWE-bench Verified, 10 randomly selected public submissions predict the median ratio for 119 other submissions within 3% for 2 or more repositories, and 3 submissions are nearly as good. Dropping the finite-population terms from the design prediction gives errors of 13-21% on GSM-Symbolic, where it reduces to the textbook formula, and 25-35% on SWE-bench. Widening iid intervals by the square root of the pilot design effect brings pass@1 coverage on concentrated designs to 0.93-0.98, but not pass@16 (0.85, 0.76). We also report two lessons for anyone validating such predictions: split pilot and held-out data by question source, not by difficulty version, and do not read a good fit of the formula as evidence of source clustering (MATH-500). The method is not new; we contribute a held-out test of its advance predictions and a recipe for using them. Code: https://github.com/Guang627/deff-eval

Machine Learning 2.title: Improved Sample Complexity of Robust Reinforcement Learning with KL Uncertainty Sets
Machine Learning 2.summary: In this paper, we study distributionally robust reinforcement learning with Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence-defined uncertainty sets. The goal is to find a policy that maximizes the robust value function, defined as the worst-case value over all transition kernels in the uncertainty set. Assuming access to a generative model, we aim to understand the sample complexity of finding an $ε$-optimal robust policy. The best-known sample complexity results in the literature show a non-trivial gap of $\mathcal{O}\{\max\{p_\wedge^{-1}(1-γ)^{-1},(1-γ)^{-2}\}\}$ between the upper and lower bounds, where $p_\wedge$ denotes the minimum positive transition probability of the nominal transition kernel, and $γ$ is the discount factor. More importantly, existing results on the lower bound only cover a limited range of the uncertainty level. In this paper, we develop tighter and complete upper and lower bounds for robust RL with KL-defined uncertainty sets. Our upper bound is the tightest among all existing studies, and it improves upon the best-known bound by at least the order of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{p_\wedge^{-1},(1-γ)^{-1}\})$ for uncertainty level $δ\in(0,1)$. Furthermore, our lower bound holds for any uncertainty level. Our upper and lower bounds (nearly) match in various regimes, providing improved results for this problem.

Machine Learning 2.title: Amortizing Exact Orthogonality: Drift-Triggered Restoration for Orthogonal Fine-Tuning
Machine Learning 2.summary: Orthogonal finetuning (OFT) adapts a pretrained weight by an orthogonal transform and preserves its singular values and row angles, but existing methods construct an exact or approximate orthogonal transform at every optimization step. We measure how far a transform $A$ is from orthogonal by its orthogonality defect $\|A^\top A-I\|_2$. For OFTv2, which truncates a Cayley-Neumann series, we show that the truncation order does not determine the defect. At its default order, block defects in checkpoints from the reference implementation span five orders of magnitude. We propose Restarted Tangent Orthogonal Finetuning (RTOFT), which uses the first-order update $W(I+S)$ of a weight $W$ with a skew-symmetric $S$ and restores exact orthogonality by a polar decomposition only when the drift $\|S\|_2$ reaches a tolerance $τ$. The defect of $I+S$ is exactly $\|S\|_2^2$. Therefore, reading the drift after every update and restoring before the next forward pass guarantees a defect of at most $τ^2$ in every forward pass, independently of the loss, data, model, and optimizer. A final restoration makes the returned transform exactly orthogonal. On GLUE, RTOFT reduces the training time of block-diagonal, subspace, and butterfly parameterizations from $1.10$-$1.58\times$ to $0.97$-$1.13\times$ that of LoRA, and its block-diagonal version exceeds LoRA by $1.98\pm0.39$ points on the six-task average over five seeds. At $τ=0.10$, the largest drift read during training stays between $0.10$ and $0.12$ across DeBERTaV3, Qwen, and diffusion models, whereas it ranges from $0.17$ to $1.65$ when restoring once per epoch. In all seven settings of our ablation, the tangent update is worse without restoration than with it, and restoring after every step yields no measurable accuracy gain over restoring at the tolerance and costs $4.5$-$27.5\%$ more per step.

Machine Learning 2.title: Sampling with graph wavelet kernels: optimality and adaptivity to regularity and geometry
Machine Learning 2.summary: We construct wavelet-based determinantal samplers on manifolds and geometric graphs whose approximation rates adapt to the regularity of the observable. On a Riemannian manifold of dimension $m$, our wavelet DPPs satisfy variance reduction of order $n^{1-2s/m}$ for linear statistics of both $s$-Hölder and $H^s$ observables, where $0<s\le1$. Using these samplers, we further construct unbiased quadrature rules with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$ using at most $3n/2$ function evaluations, matching the classical optimal randomized integration exponent. For point clouds sampled from an $m$-dimensional manifold, we develop corresponding determinantal samplers on two standard classes of geometric random graphs: $\varepsilon$-graphs and symmetric $k$-nearest-neighbour graphs. These samplers satisfy the same variance reduction for linear statistics of $s$-Hölder observables and yield conditionally unbiased estimators of empirical averages with root mean square error $O(n^{-1/2-s/m})$, using at most $2n$ function evaluations. In both settings, the rates are governed by the intrinsic dimension $m$ and the regularity $s$ of the observable.

Machine Learning 2.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: A Statistical Perspective
Machine Learning 2.summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a central framework for aligning large language models (LLMs) with human preferences. Despite its practical success, RLHF raises fundamental statistical questions because it relies on noisy, subjective, and heterogeneous feedback to learn reward models and optimize policies. This survey provides a statistical perspective on RLHF, focusing primarily on LLM alignment. We introduce the main components of RLHF, including supervised fine-tuning, reward modeling, and policy optimization, and relate them to familiar statistical concepts such as the Bradley-Terry-Luce (BTL) model, latent utility estimation, active learning, experimental design, and uncertainty quantification. We review methods for learning reward functions from pairwise preference data and for optimizing policies through both two-stage RLHF pipelines and emerging one-stage approaches such as direct preference optimization. We further discuss recent extensions including reinforcement learning from AI feedback, inference-time algorithms, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, as well as benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and open-source frameworks that support RLHF research. We conclude by highlighting open challenges in RLHF.
Machine Learning 2.comment: The paper has been accepted by Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application

Machine Learning 2.title: Externally Valid Policy Choice
Machine Learning 2.summary: We consider the problem of estimating personalized treatment policies that are "externally valid" or "generalizable": they perform well in target populations that differ from the experimental (or training) population from which the data are sampled. We first show that welfare-maximizing policies for the experimental population are robust to a certain class of shifts in the distribution of potential outcomes between the experimental and target populations (holding characteristics fixed). We then develop methods for estimating policies that are robust to shifts in the joint distribution of outcomes and characteristics. In doing so, we highlight how treatment effect heterogeneity within the experimental population shapes external validity.

Multimedia.title: Can a Short Video Clip Verify a Model Fix?
Multimedia.summary: A developer who reproduces a video model's error on a short clip can replay that clip after an update. How often does a correct clip answer mean the original test now passes? On 960 prespecified CG-Bench questions, we updated from Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct. Accuracy on a 64-frame sample spanning the full video rose from 27.9% to 33.3%. Before scoring the newer model, we froze 388 clips on which the older model reproduced its exact reference error. The updated model passed the reference on 51 of 116 clip passes (44.0%, 95% Wilson interval 35.3-53.0%) and on 16 of 272 clip failures (5.9%). Closing cases on a clip pass would have declared 65 unresolved reference failures fixed. Requiring a clip pass would have missed 16 of the 67 reference fixes (23.9%). In a separate 1,028-video study with different checkpoints and direct option scoring, only 15 clips passed, and the 16-frame reference confirmed one. For the generated-answer update, the short replay identified cases worth checking, while the original input remained necessary to verify individual fixes.
Multimedia.comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables

Multimedia.title: Multisensory Hybrid TV
Multimedia.summary: Traditional TV media content exclusively involves audiovisual streams. Multi-sensorial media (mulsemedia) introduces sensory effects such as ambient lighting, vibration, scents, wind, or temperature to stimulate other senses and create more enjoyable, realistic, and immersive content consumption experiences. This paper presents an MPEG-V- and HbbTV-based end-to-end solution for providing multi-sensorial hybrid (broadcast/broadband) TV content consumption experiences. A prototype following the proposal has been implemented on an end-to-end HbbTV-compliant platform, including both video streams and sensory effects metadata delivery and synchronous consumption, replicating a mulsemedia hybrid TV service. The prototype has been subjectively evaluated and validated by 106 participants with diverse profiles, yielding highly satisfactory results, including overall enjoyment, realism, immersion, perceived synchronization, and QoE enhancement. Furthermore, the results have also revealed interesting demographic patterns, such as participants with higher academic levels reporting lower satisfaction scores in general, distinct gender-based preferences regarding sensory acceptance, and potential barriers to commercial adoption, where higher realism and immersion do not translate into an equivalent willingness to pay for these enhanced TV services.
Multimedia.comment: 57 pages, 20 figures, 9 tables, and one Appendix qith and additional table

Multimedia.title: DiaCap: Jointly Learning Who Speaks When for Audiovisual Dialogue Captioning
Multimedia.summary: We present DiaCap, an audiovisual LLM for comprehensive dialogue captioning, which produces the transcript, timestamps, and a visual description of the speaker for every utterance in a video. Considering that utterance timing and audiovisual diarization are tightly coupled, DiaCap unifies the tasks in a single model, trained in two complementary stages. First, we train DiaCap on 225K curated clips, using synthetic captions that densely label every utterance in detail. Second, we further refine the model via reinforcement learning on 2.9K human-corrected clips, using fine-grained feedback that directly evaluates utterance timing, speaker grouping, and speaker binding. On DiaDemBench, which we extend with utterance-level timestamps and subtitle redaction, both DiaCap with off-the-shelf transcripts and its end-to-end variant DiaCap-E2E achieve strong results. Specifically, DiaCap performs on par with Gemini 4 Argon in audiovisual diarization while clearly outperforming it in timestamp accuracy (76.59 vs. 42.76 TIME). It also maintains strong diarization on multilingual and minute-long videos, and transfers to audiovisual question answering.
Multimedia.comment: 18 pages, 13 figures, 12 tables

Multimedia.title: MSRGF: Multi-Source Reconstruction with Reference-Guided Fusion for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
Multimedia.summary: Incomplete multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) predicts sentiment from textual, acoustic, and visual features when some observations are missing. Existing reconstruction methods estimate missing features from available modalities and combine the resulting information for sentiment prediction. However, different available modalities can produce distinct estimates of the same modality, while direct fusion often leaves the relationships among these estimates underused. We propose MSRGF (Multi-Source Reconstruction with Reference-Guided Fusion), which retains separate estimates and exploits their relationships during fusion. Specifically, MSRGF comprises three components: (1) Source-Wise Reconstruction (SWR), which uses modality-specific queries and a shared generator to produce a separate estimate of each modality from every available modality; (2) Reference-Guided Fusion (RGF), which uses relationships among estimates and available observations to construct a weighted reference, selectively refines it using their differences, and incorporates observed features when available; and (3) Global Context Modulation (GCM), which uses global context to adjust modality summaries for sentiment prediction. Extensive experiments on three datasets show that MSRGF outperforms existing methods, achieving average accuracy improvements of 1.9% on MOSEI under random within-modality missingness, 0.6% under random whole-modality missingness and 1.3% under fixed whole-modality missingness.
Multimedia.comment: 21 pages, 18 tables, 4 figures

Multimedia.title: Residual Guidance for Real-Time Interactive Video Generation
Multimedia.summary: Real-time interactive video generation allows users to change the prompt during generation to steer the evolving video. However, existing streaming models, which generate videos chunk by chunk, often keep following the previous prompt after a switch. We trace this failure to context inertia, where the previous chunk acts as a strong prior that suppresses the new prompt. Furthermore, we find that this inertia persists even when the cache retains only the previous chunk, yet discarding the context breaks visual continuity, which limits approaches that edit the cache. Rather than editing the cache, we propose Residual Guidance (RG), a simple, training-free method that counteracts context inertia with a correction measured outside the cache. Specifically, RG denoises the re-noised previous chunk once under the new prompt without the cache and adds the resulting residual to the early denoising steps of the next chunk, where its content is largely decided and the new prompt is most suppressed. Across settings ranging from a single switch to long multi-switch generation, RG substantially improves prompt switching capability on existing streaming models, including those with dedicated switching mechanisms, while largely retaining visual quality. As it requires no training or per-model tuning and adds only one forward pass per chunk, RG can be easily integrated into existing real-time video generation pipelines.
Multimedia.comment: Project page: https://residual-guidance.github.io

Multimedia.title: FugaStream: Pipelined Live Volumetric Streaming towards Full Exploitation of Multi-views
Multimedia.summary: Live volumetric streaming has become the cornerstone of next-generation immersive applications, enabling users to experience six degrees of freedom (6-DoF). To support interactivity, live volumetric streaming must reconstruct multi-view RGB-D frames into a unified 3D representation while meeting a stringent latency budget, where existing systems are forced to trade reconstruction quality for latency. In this paper, we present FugaStream, the first pipelined live volumetric streaming system that mitigates this trade-off by committing a base representation early and then incrementally merging novel late views. Enabling such functionalities introduces two fundamental challenges: (i) the uncertainty in frame availability, and (ii) the late view updates in a lightweight manner. We address these challenges through two key algorithms: (i) adaptive base commitment control, which determines the base commitment time with the expected reconstruction gain of each missing view against the growing cost of latency, and (ii) base-referenced late view completion, which transmits only the novel regions of late views compared to early committed base, enabling lightweight fusion at the client. We validate the effectiveness of FugaStream on a widely used volumetric dataset and a real-world testbed, demonstrating that FugaStream improves SSIM by 10.9% and IoU by 13.7% over baselines under the same 150 ms budget.
Multimedia.comment: 14 pages, 17 figures

Multimedia.title: Lossless Re-Encoding of Vorbis and Opus Audio Files
Multimedia.summary: We present Balrogg, a lossless recompressor that replaces the entropy coding of Ogg Vorbis and Ogg Opus files with adaptive context mixing models. For Vorbis, we write each represent each codebook entry as a tuple of small signed integers (digits), binarized in five stages, and mixed with a direct context model, a bit-history model, and a match model, with weights selected by the neighboring digits and the previous residue pass. For Opus, each symbol is coded by an adaptive context model initialized with the codec's probability tables as priors, and the pyramid vector quantizer (PVQ) indices of the CELT layer are split recursively into pulse counts. At the default level, Balrogg reduces Vorbis music by 16.2\%, Vorbis speech by 10.6%, and Opus speech by 5.4%; xz, zstd, ZPAQ, and bzip3 save at most 4.1% on the same files. Over 48 encoder configurations, files shrink to 66.5--96.1% of their size. Encoding and decoding are symmetric, run at 1.8--3.2~MB/s per core, and use less than 12~MiB of memory.

Multimedia.title: ViTrail: Transmission-Inference Co-Design for Vision Transformer-Based Mobile Video Analytics
Multimedia.summary: Edge-assisted mobile video analytics (MVA) relies on a tight device-edge feedback loop in which captured frames are transmitted for remote inference and the returned results are rendered on the mobile device. Many existing systems optimize frame transmission while treating server-side inference as a fixed cost. This separation becomes inefficient for vision transformer (ViT)-based dense prediction, where high-resolution inputs simultaneously increase network traffic and server computation. We present ViTrail, which co-designs transmission and ViT inference through a shared mixed-resolution representation. The device preserves task-relevant regions at full resolution and downsamples less informative regions before encoding. The server tokenizes each region at its transmitted resolution, so the same regional resolution assignment reduces both the upload payload and the number of tokens processed by the ViT. For dense prediction, ViTrail aligns regions with ViT patches and attention windows and restores a regular feature grid at a configurable stage. At runtime, it selects regional downsampling, compression quality, and the restoration point to maximize predicted installation accuracy, the accuracy of the rendered result when a new remote result is first used for rendering. We build a fully functional prototype on commodity mobile and edge devices and evaluate it in real time across 300 video-trace pairs with real-world 4G/5G traces. ViTrail achieves the highest mean rendering accuracy among the evaluated systems and leads each baseline on 81% to 95% of pairs, while reducing median end-to-end offloading latency by 38% against the most accurate baseline.
Multimedia.comment: 14 pages, 10 figures. This version substantially revises v1. The system, previously named ViTMAlis, is renamed ViTrail, its design is revised, and all experiments are redone with the revised system

Multimedia.title: A User-Item Aware Encoding Framework for Short Video
Multimedia.summary: Traditional encoding methods from the Professional Generated Content (PGC) era face significant challenges due to two unique characteristics of user-generated short videos: massive daily uploads (reaching hundreds of millions) and heterogeneous content-consumer relationships (varying video quality and diverse consumer contexts). To address these challenges, we propose UIAE (User-Item Aware Encoding), a novel multiple bitrate ladder group encoding method comprising three key components: 1) Establishing user-item relationships via rule-based or DNN-based models; 2) Developing local optimization models maximizing Quality of Experience (QoE) for sub-populations based on contextual consumption patterns; 3) Deriving globally optimal encoding strategies through hierarchical model integration. Experimental results demonstrate that the UIAE framework adaptively adjusts encoding outcomes for distinct user groups with varying context profiles, ensuring optimal QoE for end viewers. We have deployed the UIAE method into the online pipeline, handling tens of millions of video transcoding tasks daily.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted to ICASSP 2026 (ICASSP 2026 - 2026 IEEE Int. Conf. on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing). Author's preprint version, 5 pages, 4 figures, 1 table

Multimedia.title: Pothen: Can Vision-Language Models Tell Where a Cultural Object Comes From?
Multimedia.summary: A cultural object is a trace of the people who made it, and knowing who made it, where, and when shapes how it is catalogued, valued, and returned. Vision-language models now describe such objects for museum collections, yet whether they can recover this knowledge from an image has not been tested. We introduce Pothen, a benchmark of 750 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty in which a model predicts an object's title, culture, period, origin, and creator from its image alone, scored against curator-written catalogue records by an LLM judge calibrated on human annotation. Across nine models, mean field scores are 36.16% to 49.82%, but all five fields match for only 2.13% to 7.87% of objects. Images raise culture, period, and origin scores by 12.6 to 32.2 points for two models tested without them, and 83.52% of creator matches occur alongside an incorrect field. Models read visual evidence and hold facts about objects but do not bind them into one attribution, and in our error analysis their attributions follow the style an object resembles rather than the record of its making.
Multimedia.comment: 40 pages. Revised manuscript retitled Pothen, with an updated abstract and framing

Multimedia.title: Rethinking Video Agents: When and Why Video Harnesses Work
Multimedia.summary: Video understanding depends not only on how models reason about visual evidence, but also on which evidence they observe. Fixed observation policies determine this evidence in advance; agentic harnesses allow models to seek further observations as their understanding develops. This shift creates an opportunity to realize capabilities that fixed inputs leave untapped, yet the ability to request observations does not ensure their effective use. We investigate when and why video harnesses improve understanding, examining how task demands and models' capacity for interaction jointly shape their benefits. Using Video-Relook as an experimental framework, we let models adapt their temporal and spatial observations from a common default configuration, and analyze performance and interaction trajectories across models and tasks. Adaptive observation yields substantial gains on fine-grained action understanding, with benefits also extending to Video-MME-v2. Even under the same observation interface, gains differ substantially across models; interaction traces reveal corresponding differences in evidence seeking and the reliability of answer revision. The benefits also vary across tasks for the same model, ranging from substantial improvements to limited gains and regressions. Together, these findings support an account in which harness effectiveness depends on the alignment between opportunities for informative observation and the model's ability to turn interaction into reliable revisions. They motivate video harnesses that coordinate perception and reasoning, matching observational autonomy to task demands and model capabilities.

Machine Learning 2.title: Adversarial Bandit Convex Optimization with $d^{3/2}\sqrt{n}$ Regret
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study adversarial bandit convex optimization, where in each of $n$ rounds a learner chooses a point $A_t$ in a convex body $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ and observes only a noisy value of a convex loss $f_t:\mathcal{K}\to[0,1]$ at that point. The losses are chosen by an adversary, who may change them from round to round and adapt them to the learner's past actions. We improve the best known regret bound for this problem from $\widetilde O(d^{5/2}\sqrt n)$ (Lattimore, 2020, 2026) to $\widetilde O(d^{3/2}\sqrt n)$, which matches the rate conjectured by Bubeck et al. (2017). Together with the recent lower bound of $Ω(d^{4/3}\sqrt n)$ due to Rajaraman and Han (2026), it determines the minimax regret up to a factor of $d^{1/6}$ and logarithmic factors. The algorithm is an online Newton step with Gaussian exploration. Unlike earlier methods of this kind, it uses unbiased estimates of the gradient and Hessian of the Gaussian smoothing of the loss, rather than of an optimistic surrogate.

Machine Learning 2.title: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics: Observable Entropy Control under Protected-Risk Constraints
Machine Learning 2.summary: Human-Centered Learning Mechanics (HCLM) treats learning as an open, controlled process in which task progress, representation information, structural restrictions and externally specified risk limits jointly govern parameter updates. We characterise this mechanism through a normalised covariance-information force, metric observability and exact feasible rate constraints. The projected task rate depends on an observable cross-product that differs from the ordinary task information product when a probe set does not contain the training task. Error, finite-step and delay margins specify when admissible local requests can be implemented. A primary 288-run neural study separates information control from empirical risk protection and retains cases where extra compression worsens held-out loss. Follow-up experiments train the observable restriction in a declared 13-dimensional subspace, implement a frozen-public-encoder readout through an actual Gaussian sample channel, evaluate a fixed-coefficient sensitivity grid, and test targeted nuisance control with two-hidden-layer minibatch learning on Fashion-MNIST. The nuisance study improves shifted accuracy over ERM, while generic protected balancing accounts for most of the gain. Together, the theory and experiments identify attainable information actions, predictive costs and the separate assumptions required for population-risk certification.

Machine Learning 2.title: Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching
Machine Learning 2.summary: We propose Coreset-Induced Conditional Velocity Flow Matching (CCVFM), a generative model that augments hierarchical rectified flow with a data-informed source distribution. Standard flow matching regresses only the conditional mean of the velocity; hierarchical flow matching instead models the full conditional velocity law with a second, inner flow in velocity space, but this inner flow is asked to transport isotropic Gaussian noise to a multimodal target velocity distribution from scratch. Our key observation is that this inner source can be replaced by a closed-form surrogate built from a coreset of the target. CCVFM first compresses the target into weighted atoms using an entropic Sinkhorn coreset and lifts them to a Gaussian mixture. The induced conditional velocity law is then a closed-form Gaussian mixture that can be sampled without a learned neural sampler. A lightweight correction flow, trained from this surrogate source, then refines the remaining surrogate-to-target residual rather than learning an entire noise-to-data map. We prove that the surrogate transport cost equals the target-surrogate Wasserstein gap under an explicit compression assumption, whereas the noise-source analogue has a dimension-scale lower bound. We further characterize the conditional second moment of the training target when the source velocity is drawn from the surrogate law independently of the target velocity, and show that the part of it that depends on the source is small when the surrogate conditional law is close to the true conditional velocity law in mean and covariance. Empirically, on MNIST, CIFAR-10, ImageNet-32, and CelebA-HQ, the proposed method reaches competitive few-step generation under matched architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/ziwaa-se/CCVFM.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 48 pages. Code: https://github.com/ziwaa-se/CCVFM

Machine Learning 2.title: On the Impact of Extra Information in Bandit Learning: More is Not Always Merrier
Machine Learning 2.summary: More data is commonly assumed to improve learning performance, however, we show that this intuition can surprisngly fail in sequential decision-making. Considering a stochastic bandits setup with exogenous extra information, we ask if the free and unbiased extra reward samples are guaranteed to reduce the regret of the learner. We introduce a formal notion of `non-degradation under extra information' and demonstrate that the widely used Upper Confidence Bound algorithm (UCB) violates this property, i.e., there exist benign extra-information under which UCB incurs strictly higher regret than when run without extra information. We contrast this behaviour with Thompson Sampling and Explore-Then-Commit, which appear to benefit from the same extra information. Constructively, we propose a meta-algorithm that provably enforces non-degradation for a broad class of bandit algorithms. We also run empirical simulations to study our meta-algorithm.

Machine Learning 2.title: Differentially Private Policy Optimization in Linear MDPs with Adversarial Rewards
Machine Learning 2.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) in personalized services often relies on sensitive interaction data. Motivated by the need to protect these data, we study differentially private (DP) policy optimization in episodic linear Markov decision processes (MDPs) with unknown transitions and adaptive adversarial linear rewards under full-information feedback. This setting poses two key challenges: past trajectories are repeatedly reused for policy evaluation, and reward choices may depend on previously released private statistics. The proposed algorithm combines batched proximal policy optimization (PPO) updates with optimistic policy evaluation, using private regression statistics and reward estimates to protect both trajectories and reward functions under joint differential privacy (JDP). With all other parameters fixed, our high-probability regret bound retains the same leading $\widetilde{O}\left(K^{3/4}\right)$ dependence on the number of episodes $K$ as the corresponding non-private bound for batched optimistic PPO. The additional privacy terms scale as $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{5/8}\right)$ and $\widetilde{O} \left(K^{1/2}\right)$. Thus, privacy incurs only lower-order additive costs in $K$, even under adaptive adversarial rewards.

Machine Learning 2.title: CoDeQ: Compression with a Dead-Zone Quantizer for Differentiable Joint Pruning--Quantization
Machine Learning 2.summary: Joint pruning and quantization can reduce the inference cost of neural-networks, but determining layerwise sparsity and precision often requires auxiliary allocation procedures and considerable hyperparameter tuning. We introduce CoDeQ, a quantization-aware training method that unifies pruning and quantization through a learnable dead-zone quantizer. Its learned dead-zone width controls layerwise sparsity, while bit widths can be held fixed or learned in mixed-precision mode. A pruning-aware scale allocates all available nonzero reconstruction levels over the retained range. We derive the spacing that minimizes worst-case reconstruction error over this range for a fixed bit width and range endpoint. Model weights and compression parameters are optimized jointly under one global compression coefficient, with a shared learning rate for the compression parameters. On VGG7/CIFAR-10, CoDeQ with 2-bit activations achieves 0.05% relative BOPs, for an accuracy drop of 0.32 percentage points. On DeiT-Tiny/ImageNet-1K, mixed-precision CoDeQ preserves FP32-level accuracy at only 8.12% relative BOPs. Additional experiments across several architectures and datasets demonstrate competitive accuracy--BOP trade-offs against other joint compression methods.

Machine Learning 2.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
Machine Learning 2.summary:
The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory.
  To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner.
  We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

Machine Learning 2.title: BayesFlow 2: Multi-Backend Amortized Bayesian Inference in Python
Machine Learning 2.summary: Modern Bayesian inference involves a mixture of computational methods for estimating, validating, and drawing conclusions from probabilistic models as part of principled workflows. An overarching motif of many Bayesian methods is that they are relatively slow, which often becomes prohibitive when fitting complex models to large data sets. Amortized Bayesian inference (ABI) offers a path to solving the computational challenges of Bayes. ABI trains neural networks on model simulations, rewarding users with rapid inference of any model-implied quantity, such as point estimates, likelihoods, or full posterior distributions. In this work, we present the Python library BayesFlow, Version 2, for general-purpose ABI. Along with direct posterior, likelihood, and ratio estimation, the software includes support for multiple popular deep learning backends, a rich collection of generative networks for sampling and density estimation, complete customization and high-level interfaces, as well as new capabilities for hyperparameter optimization, design optimization, and multilevel modeling. Using a case study on dynamical system parameter estimation, combined with comparisons to similar software, we show that our streamlined, user-friendly workflow has strong potential to support broad adoption.

Machine Learning 2.title: Centered Kernel Distance: Dimension-Free Error Bounds for Comparing Neural Representations
Machine Learning 2.summary: The asymptotic error of representational similarity metrics such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) and representational similarity analysis (RSA) has been well-characterized, but there are no realistic bounds on how estimates of representational similarity $\textit{simultaneously}$ depend on the number of sampled neurons ($N$) and experimental conditions ($M$). We study the natural metric counterpart of CKA and RSA, which we call the Centered Kernel Distance (CKD). We show that CKD admits an unbiased estimator, whereas several popular similarity measures including CKA have no unbiased estimator. Under mild assumptions, we show that estimation error of CKD decays in proportion to $1/M + 1/N$. Strikingly, the rate in this bound does not depend on the dimensionality of the space of experimental conditions. Thus, similarity estimation does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality, which plagues similar problems in high-dimensional statistics. We verify our results empirically in random shallow neural networks, trained neural networks, and macaque visual cortex data. Ultimately, this paper advances a framework for predicting the error of similarity estimators in experiments by relaxing existing, biologically-unrealistic assumptions. Our theoretical and empirical predictions produce specific prescriptions on how to most efficiently estimate the similarity between multiple neural systems.
Machine Learning 2.comment: 11 pages (48 total), 3 figures (15 total), submitted to ICLR 2027

Machine Learning 2.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Under a Generative Model
Machine Learning 2.summary: Reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how an agent interacts with an environment in order to extract as large a reward as possible. A standard approach to study such interaction is through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the task of choosing an optimal policy---a function that tells the agent which action to take. In this work, we study two types of time-dependent MDP---finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted---and propose new quantum algorithms for computing approximate optimal policies. Our quantum algorithms are based on a new combination of standard value iteration and quantum subroutines like quantum mean estimation and quantum maximum finding, overall enhanced with techniques from sample-optimal classical algorithms. Our resulting query complexities improve upon previous works, thus approaching already established quantum lower bounds.
Machine Learning 2.comment: 23 pages. v2: added references, rewrote several parts of the paper, fixed a bug in the main theorems, generalised the results on discounted MDPs to the time-dependent setting

Machine Learning 2.title: Can Tabular In-Context Learners Generalize to Biomolecular Property Prediction?
Machine Learning 2.summary: Predicting biomolecular properties from limited labeled data is a central bottleneck in protein engineering and small-molecule design. As strong pretrained encoders now supply rich fixed-length representations, the difficulty has shifted from representation learning to building a data-efficient predictor for the few-shot regime. Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN and TabICL perform this prediction through in-context inference after pretraining on synthetic tables. We test whether they can act as flexible interpolators over informative fixed biomolecular representations. Treating each method as a predictor-representation pair, we evaluate across two domains. On ProteinGym, TabPFN3-ESMC600M is competitive with leading supervised-substitution entries and obtains the lowest MSE among the leaderboard-context rows considered, while Kermut remains stronger by Spearman. Performance is substantially lower under modulo and contiguous holdouts than under random splits. On the five-endpoint PpEST dataset, tabular models show favorable descriptive performance against matched supervised baselines, but the random split measures within-family interpolation and the small endpoint count precludes strong model-ordering claims. For small-molecule classification with ECFP/RDKit descriptors, no single predictor-representation pairing dominates across TDC ADMET, MoleculeNet, FS-Mol, and DrugOOD, but several pairings are competitive with strong descriptor and graph baselines. Crucially, on both protein and small-molecule few-shot tasks, these predictor-representation pairs offer strong performance. We conclude that tabular foundation models can be strong biomolecular predictors, but only when coupled with expressive representations.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Accepted at the Asian Conference on Machine Learning (ACML 2026)

Machine Learning 2.title: Gaussian priors from nonlinear PDEs with the semiclassical approximation
Machine Learning 2.summary: Probabilistic numerical methods for partial differential equations (PDE) combines the governing physics with observations to treat solving the PDE as a Bayesian inverse problem. This allows techniques to quantify the uncertainty in the field reconstruction under model-form error. In the majority of cases, a Gaussian prior is assigned to the field of interest, and Bayes's theorem in the infinite-dimensional setting is used to derive the posterior. While Gaussians have been shown to be well-suited for linear PDEs, a similar treatment for nonlinear PDEs remains open-ended. In this work, study the use of the semiclassical approximation to construct Gaussian priors from variational energies or integrated square residuals for probabilistic numerics. The prior is derived by expanding the PDE energy about a stable solution and uncovering a Gaussian form. We then analyze the different characteristics of the resulting priors as they pertain to the inverse problem. In particular, we find that the covariance operator is given by the inverse of the Hessian of the energy whose associated Cameron-Martin space is the solution space of the PDE. We also find that the prior responds to model-form error by sharpening or flattening itself depending on the distance between the ground truth and the solution of the assumed model.

Machine Learning 2.title: Evaluating Ensemble Methods for Algorithmic Stability Under Data Perturbations
Machine Learning 2.summary: Standard classification algorithms often exhibit sensitivity near decision boundaries, which can compound instability that already exists from overfitting to a subset of high-influence samples. Ensembling is commonly used to stabilize classifiers, but we show that it can destabilize those that are already stable. The well-established practice of subbagging can yield substantial improvements in stability, as we validate in the cause-of-death classification setting. However, its effect depends on the perturbation level, and for stable classifiers the finite number of bags introduces destabilizing Monte Carlo noise that shrinks only slowly as the number of bags grows. This instability can be mitigated, though, by the recently proposed inflated argmax, which allows for multi-class predictions in ambiguous cases. We further examine the extent to which the Rashomon set, the collection of distinct models that achieve near-optimal predictive performance, can reduce instability by leveraging predictive multiplicity rather than resampling. We find that the Rashomon ensemble can stabilize unstable classifiers, but requires sufficient predictive multiplicity, which is not guaranteed. It is a promising direction, but not currently a general substitute for subbagging. Our results are consistent with an influence equalization interpretation of why these ensemble approaches stabilize unstable classifiers, although their failures on stable classifiers appear to have distinct sources.

Machine Learning 2.title: Concentration Inequalities for Exchangeable Tensors and Matrix-valued Data
Machine Learning 2.summary:
We study concentration inequalities for structured weighted sums of random data, including (i) tensor inner products and (ii) sequential matrix sums. We are interested in tail bounds and concentration inequalities for those structured weighted sums under exchangeability, extending beyond the classical framework of independent terms.
  We develop Hoeffding and Bernstein bounds provided with structure-dependent exchangeability. Along the way, we recover known results in weighted sum of exchangeable random variables and i.i.d. sums of random matrices to the optimal constants. We also derive a concentration bound for combinatorial sums of matrix arrays with an improved constant in the bias term compared with that by the method of exchangeable pairs.
  For applications, the richer structures provide us with novel analytical tools for estimating the average effect of multi-factor response models and studying fixed-design sketching methods in federated averaging. We apply our results to these problems, and find that our theoretical predictions are corroborated by numerical evidence.
Machine Learning 2.comment: 49 pages, 3 figures. Accepted for publication in the SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science (SIMODS)

Machine Learning 2.title: Two Timescales of Forgetting in Fine-tuning of Language Models: Fast Behavioral Suppression and Slow Representational Drift
Machine Learning 2.summary: Today, a core pipeline of artificial intelligence systems is pretraining on a broad range of text corpora and then fine-tuning on specific tasks or desired behaviors. Yet we still have limited understanding of how fine-tuning on a restricted data distribution modifies representations acquired during pretraining. In particular, it remains unclear whether surface behavioral suppression happens together with the erasure of latent representations that support it. In this work, we study supervised fine-tuning (SFT) by pretraining transformers on a controlled context-free grammar with hierarchical latent structure, the Random Hierarchy Model (RHM), and fine-tuning with a restricted subset of its generative rules. While during pretraining the model's ability to generate with the correct grammar rules coincides with building the internal representations of the corresponding latent, we find that SFT exhibits a very different dynamics: (i) the generation of deleted rules changes on a fast timescale inversely proportional to the magnitude of the token-latent correlation; meanwhile, their corresponding representations stay intact; (ii) the hidden representations of the deleted rules become forgotten on a much longer timescale, associated with a slow drift of the network parameters. Finally, we observe analogous results in a realistic setup with natural language, suggesting that this timescale separation in forgetting is a more general phenomenon of fine-tuning language models.

Machine Learning 2.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
Machine Learning 2.summary: A prediction interval should contain the outcome at a stated rate. Conformal prediction sets its width from past forecast errors. When the process behind a time series changes on an announced date, intervals set from errors before that break can stop covering. After Australia moved to five minute electricity settlement, a 90% interval fixed beforehand covered 51.5% of the next 400 days. One forecaster needs the next interval to cover, another a finished period's share of misses at 10%. We show that each need calls for its own restart at the date. We recompute the next interval from the $n$ errors since the break. If these errors are independent, its coverage comes within $O(n^{-1/2})$ of the stated rate, the best order attainable. For a finished period, we restart adaptive conformal inference (ACI). On bounded errors, if a floor under its width adds a bounded total, it brings the share of misses within $O(n^{-1})$ of target but promises nothing about the next interval. After a simulated mean shift of 5.0 noise standard deviations, recomputed intervals cover within 3.5 percentage points of 90% on average at the 50th forecast, a third closer than the 5.2 of the best of five baselines. Of nine announced breaks in power markets and at a central bank, restarting ACI gives a detectable gain only at the one large break.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). 44 pages, 8 figures

Machine Learning 2.title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning
Machine Learning 2.summary: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.

Machine Learning 2.title: Jacobian-Velocity Bounds for Deployment Risk Under Covariate Drift
Machine Learning 2.summary: We study long-horizon deployment of a frozen predictor under dynamic covariate shift. A time-domain Poincaré inequality first reduces temporal risk volatility to derivative energy, and a Jacobian-velocity theorem supplies the corresponding pathwise control. A remainder extension separates the model-mediated, controllable term from conditional-risk variation not transmitted through the score Jacobian. Under low-rank drift, the bound decomposes the controllable term into tangent energy parallel and orthogonal to the drift subspace. This motivates drift-aligned tangent regularization (DTR), its anisotropic extension with a weaker orthogonal guardrail, and a matched monitoring proxy. Controlled experiments verify the temporal inequality, the efficiency of directional smoothing, and the necessity of the remainder term. The main field study uses a 128-dimensional gas-sensor array over ten chronological batches. A rank-4 basis estimated entirely before deployment beats ten matched random subspaces, and validation-selected anisotropic DTR improves deployment cross-entropy and volatility over pure DTR in all ten matched seeds while retaining substantially more accuracy than isotropic smoothing. Air Quality and power-consumption studies provide complementary regression evidence. Together, the results support a precise design rule: concentrate smoothness along expected motion, and use limited orthogonal smoothing when the estimated drift subspace may be incomplete.

Machine Learning 2.title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
Machine Learning 2.summary: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.
Machine Learning 2.comment: 27 pages, 5 figures. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 11/2026. Reviewed on OpenReview: https://openreview.net/forum?id=GXDe6REdu3

Machine Learning 2.title: Online V-Learning with Adaptive Longitudinal Data
Machine Learning 2.summary: Reinforcement learning methods for estimating optimal dynamic treatment regimes are increasingly applied in mobile health (mHealth), where treatment decisions are made continually. Luckett et al. (2020) proposed V-learning, which estimates an optimal policy from offline trajectories. In practice, mHealth policies are updated online. Batch updating, in which the policy is re-estimated after each block of new data, is a tractable middle ground between offline learning and updating after every observation. However, because each batch's treatment policy is estimated from data pooled across patients in earlier batches, the resulting data are adaptively collected and patient trajectories are dependent, a setting that offline theory does not address. We develop statistical theory for V-learning in this setting with varying, deterministic batch sizes. For each fixed batch, as the number of patients grows, we establish uniform consistency of the estimated value function, consistency of the estimated policy, a functional central limit theorem over the policy class, asymptotic normality of the estimated value of the learned policy, and a consistent variance estimator. To first order, the online procedure performs as well as an oracle that deploys the optimal policy after the first batch. With the number of patients fixed and the number of batches growing, the estimated value function and policy remain consistent under a persistent identifiability condition. In simulations, as the number of patients grows with the number of batches fixed, confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage under adaptive assignment and the online procedure closely matches the oracle. With a small cohort followed over many batches, the learned policies improve steadily.

Machine Learning 2.title: PHM-ensemble: Scalable and Stable Probabilistic Multiresolution Clustering via Ensemble Density Estimation
Machine Learning 2.summary: Clustering is a foundational tool for exploratory data analysis across the sciences. We argue that clustering methods should be evaluated along four dimensions: fidelity to the data's underlying structure, interpretability of the recovered groups, stability under data perturbations and algorithmic randomness, and scalability to modern scientific datasets. Yet existing methods rarely satisfy all four criteria. To address this gap, we introduce PHM-ensemble, a general probabilistic framework for multiresolution clustering that estimates the underlying data density by pooling mixture models from an ensemble of fits and subsequently constructs a clustering hierarchy through hierarchical merging of the mixture components. On simulated datasets and the MNIST benchmark, PHM-ensemble matches or outperforms widely used clustering algorithms in agreement with ground truth, produces more stable results across runs, and reveals complex underlying structures. Applied to 1.82 million peripheral blood cells from the Human Immune Health Atlas, PHM-ensemble achieves higher agreement with expert-curated major cell-type annotations than the Leiden clustering used in the original study (adjusted Rand index 0.965 versus 0.789), while requiring only half the computing time. Beyond identifying major immune lineages, it reveals biologically coherent relationships among cell types and resolves finer structure within individual lineages, uncovering subtypes and cellular states consistent with known biology.

Machine Learning 2.title: B-SLIM: BART Sparse Linear Interactions Model for Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
Machine Learning 2.summary: Estimating covariate-dependent treatment effects is a central challenge in personalized medicine. Existing approaches often emphasize either fully parametric models, risking misspecification, or flexible machine learning methods, which may require large samples to detect the small treatment effect heterogeneity common in medical settings. We propose B-SLIM (BART Sparse Linear Interaction Model), a semi-parametric model for causal inference that combines a flexible Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) prognostic component with a sparse linear treatment effect component. This hybrid structure combines flexible prognosis modelling with interpretable treatment effects. The treatment effect component includes main effects and pairwise interactions, regularized through a global-local shrinkage prior. The model allows covariates to contribute to both components and provides direct inference on treatment effect modifiers, conditional mean potential outcomes, and conditional average treatment effects (CATEs). In simulations, B-SLIM outperforms a fully non-parametric alternative when main effects and pairwise interactions adequately represent the treatment effect function, whereas the non-parametric model performs better under strong non-linearity. On the nonlinear Infant Health and Development Program (IHDP) benchmark, the two Bayesian methods are competitive in predictive accuracy and ranking, and both achieve lower mean CATE error than the DR-learner, S-learner, and R-learner implementations considered. In the CANVAS trials, both methods yield similar rankings, while B-SLIM identifies several important drivers of treatment effect heterogeneity. B-SLIM enables interpretable inference on treatment effect parameters and patient-specific prediction of conditional mean potential outcomes, while remaining competitive at sample sizes relevant to medical studies.

Machine Learning 2.title: A Unified Heat-Ball Framework for Fokker--Planck Equations: Mean-Value Identities, Exact Sampling, and Error Analysis
Machine Learning 2.summary: Diffusion-based generative models with nonlinear or learned forward drifts raise questions that stay hidden for Gaussian forward processes: how the divergence-free and gradient parts of the drift shape the evolving density, whether sampling can draw on local rather than global information, and how to treat low-density regions, where $u$ carries a weak signal while $\log u$ diverges and the entropy density $u\log u$ falls between the two. These questions motivate the present study of local representations for Fokker--Planck equations with general, possibly nonlinear and time-dependent drift. We derive inhomogeneous heat-ball identities for the density $u$, the log-density $\log u$, the entropy density $u\log u$, and the score $\nabla\log u$, keeping the source terms generated by the drift; their unscaled residuals recover the corresponding differential residuals at leading order in the squared heat-ball radius. The weights appearing in the identities, the source integrals, and the integration-by-parts formulas all belong to a single Beta--Gamma family of measures on the heat ball, which gives exact rejection-free sampling, product quadrature, and unbiased Monte Carlo estimators with variance and cost bounds that are explicit in the dimension and the radius. Experiments with Gaussian-mixture and nonlinear-drift references, in dimensions up to $1024$ where applicable, confirm the sampling laws, the identities, and the residual behavior. In particular, log-density and score evaluations remain accurate where direct density estimation breaks down, and the heat-ball residuals provide local consistency tests for learned score models. A study of gauge-based heat-ball walks illustrates a recursive use of the density identity.

Machine Learning 2.title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
Machine Learning 2.summary: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.

Machine Learning 2.title: $K$-Midranks: A robust clustering algorithm for heavy-tailed data with applications to spectroscopy and finance
Machine Learning 2.summary: Clustering data with extreme observations and heavy tails can be challenging for methods that rely on distances between raw observations or specific distributional assumptions. We introduce $K$-midranks, a clustering method that replaces observations with coordinatewise ranks and partitions the transformed data using a procedure analogous to $K$-means. This transformation reduces the influence of extreme values while preserving the ordering of observations within each variable. We evaluate $K$-midranks against $K$-means, $K$-medoids, and mixture models based on Gaussian, Student's t, Cauchy, and generalized hyperbolic distributions through simulation studies, and provide some theoretical properties. $K$-midranks generally outperforms the competing methods on Cauchy-shifted data. In contrast, $K$-means and model-based methods perform better on Gaussian data and Student's t data with three degrees of freedom. We demonstrate the method's practical use in grouping samples based on Raman and LIBS spectra and clustering S\&P 500 stocks according to their returns. $K$-midranks achieves competitive performance with model-based methods in the spectroscopy applications and the best performance among the methods considered in the stock-return application. These findings suggest that $K$-midranks provides a useful alternative for clustering data with Cauchy-like heavy tails. An R package implementing the proposed method is available.
Machine Learning 2.comment: 36 pages with a 6-page supplement. Supplementary material is now available as a PDF for easier access. The main manuscript remains unchanged

Machine Learning 2.title: Efficient Prediction of pass@k Scaling in Large Language Models
Machine Learning 2.summary: Assessing the capabilities and risks of frontier AI systems is a critical area of research; recent work has shown that repeated sampling can dramatically increase both. For instance, repeated sampling allows models to solve difficult math and coding problems, but it may also increase their risk of being jailbroken. Such results raise a crucial question: how can one accurately predict a model's behavior when scaled to a massive number of attempts, given a vastly smaller sampling budget? This question is directly relevant to model providers, who serve hundreds of millions of users daily, and to governmental regulators, who seek to prevent harms. To answer this question, we make three contributions. First, we find that standard methods for fitting these laws suffer from statistical shortcomings that hinder predictions, especially in data-limited scenarios. Second, we remedy these shortcomings by introducing a robust estimation framework, which uses a beta-binomial distribution to generate more accurate predictions from limited data. Third, we propose a dynamic sampling strategy that allocates a greater budget to harder problems. Combined, these innovations enable more reliable prediction of rare risks and capabilities at a fraction of the computational cost.

Machine Learning 2.title: qshap: Fast Shapley Decomposition of $R^2$ for Gradient-Boosted Trees
Machine Learning 2.summary: Numerous methods have been developed to quantify feature attributions in individual predictions for tree ensembles. However, many applications require global measures of feature contributions to overall model performance. Although local attribution scores can be aggregated to characterize feature importance, such summaries do not directly decompose measures of predictive performance, such as $R^2$. This article introduces qshap, available in both R and Python, which provides Shapley decomposition of $R^2$ values for gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs) to quantify feature-specific contributions to model performance. By decomposing the quadratic loss of individual observations, qshap provides flexible tools to explore the importance of individual features and observations. qshap currently supports widely used GBDT implementations, including xgboost, lightgbm, and catboost, through a unified tree representation and efficient C++ backends. Its modular design can accommodate other GBDT implementations built from binary decision trees. In addition, we introduce a specialized backend for oblivious trees that exploits their symmetric structure to substantially accelerate computation.

Machine Learning 2.title: Weak instrumental variables due to ignored nonlinearities in panel data: An Orthogonal Super Learner Control Function estimator
Machine Learning 2.summary: A triangular structural panel data model with additively separable individual-specific effects is used to model the causal effect of a covariate on an outcome variable when there are unobservable confounders with some of them time-invariant. In this setup, a linear specification for the reduced-form equation might be problematic when the conditional mean of the endogenous covariate and the instrumental variables is nonlinear in the population. The reason is that ignoring the nonlinearity could lead to weak instruments (instruments are weakly correlated with the endogenous covariate) due to misspecification as shown using a generalized concentration parameter for panel data. As a solution, we propose a triangular simultaneous equation model for panel data with additive separable individual-specific fixed effects composed of a linear structural equation with a nonlinear reduced form equation. The parameter of interest is the structural parameter of the endogenous variable. The identification of this parameter is obtained under the assumption of available exclusion restrictions and using a control function approach. We derive a Neyman orthogonal score, and we provide an estimator that we call Orthogonal Super Learner Control Function (Orthogonal SLCF) estimator. The estimation procedure is composed of two main steps and cross-fitting. First, we estimate the control function using a super learner. In the following step, we use the estimated control function to control for endogeneity in the structural equation. Cross-fitting is done across the individual dimension. The estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal achieving a parametric rate of convergence. We show that the Orthogonal SLCF estimator is equivalent to the plug-in IV estimator but not equivalent to the naive plug-in 2SLS estimator which is not root-NT consistent.

Machine Learning 2.title: Beyond Point Forecasts: A Survey on Probabilistic Forecasting for Time Series and Spatiotemporal Data
Machine Learning 2.summary: Probabilistic forecasting is central to decision-making under uncertainty, yet its methodological landscape has become increasingly fragmented across temporal and spatiotemporal forecasting, statistical modeling, machine learning, and deep generative modeling. This survey develops a unified perspective by organizing probabilistic forecasting methods according to where and how uncertainty is introduced into the forecasting pipeline. Our taxonomy connects model-agnostic approaches including ensembles and distribution-free calibration, with model-intrinsic approaches spanning Bayesian modeling, parametric predictive distributions, distributional regression, and modern generative models, and further examines the emerging role of time series foundation models. Beyond methodological synthesis, we identify the assumptions, computational demands, and forms of uncertainty represented by different paradigms, and translate these distinctions into data-driven and domain-specific guidance for method selection. We complement the survey with a cross-paradigm empirical study on univariate, multivariate, and spatiotemporal forecasting tasks. The results reveal that no single uncertainty-quantification paradigm dominates across settings. Calibration, sharpness, predictive accuracy, and computational efficiency can lead to substantially different model preferences, while expressive generative models and zero-shot foundation models exhibit markedly different accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. Lastly, we identify unresolved challenges surrounding uncertainty in evolving dependency structures, physics-informed predictive distributions, forecasting extreme events, handling count-valued, directional, and continuous-time series, and the development of unified software resources. Our survey provides both a conceptual framework and a practical roadmap for probabilistic forecasting research.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (11/2026). OpenReview version available at https://openreview.net/forum?id=F140ECa1HO

Machine Learning 2.title: Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoders for Scalable Phenotyping of Health Trajectories
Machine Learning 2.summary: Clustering longitudinal health trajectories requires handling high-dimensional measurements, irregular visit times, and subject-level heterogeneity while retaining clinically interpretable structure. Existing methods address this only partially: latent-class mixed models yield an interpretable, covariate-driven partition but do not scale past a handful of markers, while deep time-series clustering scales at the cost of that structure and generally requires a common time grid. We introduce the Latent Class Mixed Model Variational Autoencoder (LCMM-VAE), a deep generative model whose latent prior is a mixture of class-specific linear mixed models, so that each subject's latent trajectory decomposes into its class mean trajectory and a subject-specific deviation. We derive a variational EM algorithm whose class responsibilities, random effects and mixed-model parameters are updated in closed form, and provide identifiability guarantees under stated conditions. Experiments on simulated and real longitudinal cohorts show that LCMM-VAE returns a partition, a reconstruction of incomplete trajectories and interpretable class-level dynamics at once, while remaining competitive with classical and deep baselines.
Machine Learning 2.comment: Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026, Proceedings track

Machine Learning 2.title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
Machine Learning 2.summary: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

Machine Learning 2.title: Seldon TFM family: Seldon-Mini, Seldon and Seldon+
Machine Learning 2.summary: We introduce Seldon, a family of tabular foundation models. Our classifier Seldon+ ranks first among 15 models on TabBench, our benchmark of 124 classification datasets, and on its variant with missing values. In our own runs of public benchmarks, it also ranks first on BeyondArena IID classification and TabBench-Bio, and second on TabArena classification. The open-weight models Seldon-Mini (27M parameters) and Seldon (213M parameters) both lie on the TabArena Pareto front of Elo against inference time: no entry is both more accurate and faster. On TabArena, Seldon ranks fourth and Seldon-Mini seventh among 109 leaderboard entries, and on the IID track of BeyondArena, Seldon ranks second among 42 entries. Seldon-Mini and Seldon handle both classification and regression, use an architecture similar to those of Kumo-Tabular, TabFM and TabPFN-3.5, and are trained on synthetic tables only.
